sections.h: Religious reform, women, the poor and print in India
sections.md:
**Religious reform and public debates.** From the early nineteenth century there were intense debates around religious issues. Different groups confronted the changes happening within colonial society in different ways and offered a variety of new interpretations of the beliefs of different religions. Some criticised existing practices and campaigned for reform, while others countered the arguments of reformers. These debates were carried out in public and in print. Printed tracts and newspapers not only spread the new ideas, but shaped the nature of the debate. A wider public could now participate in these public discussions and express their views. New ideas emerged through these clashes of opinions.

This was a time of intense controversies between social and religious reformers and the Hindu orthodoxy over matters like **widow immolation, monotheism, Brahmanical priesthood and idolatry**. In Bengal, as the debate developed, tracts and newspapers proliferated, circulating a variety of arguments. To reach a wider audience, the ideas were printed in the everyday, spoken language of ordinary people. **Rammohun Roy** published the ***Sambad Kaumudi*** from **1821** and the Hindu orthodoxy commissioned the ***Samachar Chandrika*** to oppose his opinions. From 1822, two Persian newspapers were published, ***Jam-i-Jahan Nama*** and ***Shamsul Akhbar***. In the same year, a Gujarati newspaper, the ***Bombay Samachar***, made its appearance.

In north India, the **ulama** were deeply anxious about the collapse of Muslim dynasties. They feared that colonial rulers would encourage conversion and change the Muslim personal laws. To counter this, they used cheap lithographic presses, published Persian and Urdu translations of holy scriptures, and printed religious newspapers and tracts. The **Deoband Seminary**, founded in **1867**, published thousands upon thousands of **fatwas** telling Muslim readers how to conduct themselves in their everyday lives, and explaining the meanings of Islamic doctrines.

Among Hindus, too, print encouraged the reading of religious texts, especially in the vernacular languages. The first printed edition of the ***Ramcharitmanas* of Tulsidas**, a sixteenth-century text, came out from **Calcutta in 1810**. By the mid-nineteenth century, cheap lithographic editions flooded north Indian markets. From the 1880s, the **Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow** and the **Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay** published numerous religious texts in vernaculars. In their printed and portable form, these could be read easily by the faithful at any place and time. They could also be read out to large groups of illiterate men and women.

Print did not only stimulate the publication of conflicting opinions amongst communities, but it also **connected communities and people in different parts of India**. Newspapers conveyed news from one place to another, creating pan-Indian identities.

**New forms of publication.** Printing created an appetite for new kinds of writing. As more and more people could now read, they wanted to see their own lives, experiences, emotions and relationships reflected in what they read. The **novel**, a literary firm which had developed in Europe, ideally catered to this need. It soon acquired distinctively Indian forms and styles. Other new literary forms also entered the world of reading — lyrics, short stories, essays about social and political matters. By the end of the nineteenth century, a new **visual culture** was taking shape. Painters like **Raja Ravi Varma** produced images for mass circulation. Cheap prints and calendars were easily available in the bazaar. By the 1870s, **caricatures and cartoons** were being published in journals and newspapers, commenting on social and political issues.

**Women and print.** Lives and feelings of women began to be written in particularly vivid and intense ways. Women's reading therefore increased enormously in middle-class homes. Liberal husbands and fathers began educating their womenfolk at home and sent them to schools when women's schools were set up in the cities and towns after the mid-nineteenth century. Many journals began carrying writings by women, and explained why women should be educated. But not all families were liberal. Conservative Hindus believed that a literate girl would be widowed, and Muslims feared that educated women would be corrupted by reading Urdu romances. Sometimes, rebel women defied such prohibition. **Rashsundari Debi**, a young married girl in a very orthodox household in East Bengal, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen. Later she wrote her autobiography ***Amar Jiban***, published in **1876** — the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language.

Since social reforms and novels had already created a great interest in women's lives and emotions, there was also an interest in what women would have to say about their own lives. From the 1860s, a few Bengali women like **Kailashbashini Debi** wrote books highlighting the experiences of women — about how women were imprisoned at home, kept in ignorance, forced to do hard domestic labour and treated unjustly by the very people they served. In the 1880s, in present-day Maharashtra, **Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai** wrote with passionate anger about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows. A woman in a Tamil novel expressed what reading meant to women who were so greatly confined by social regulations: 'For various reasons, my world is small… More than half my life's happiness has come from books…'

In the early twentieth century, journals written for and sometimes edited by women became extremely popular. They discussed issues like women's education, widowhood, widow remarriage and the national movement. In Punjab, **Ram Chaddha** published the fast-selling ***Istri Dharm Vichar*** to teach women how to be obedient wives. In Bengal, an entire area in central Calcutta — the **Battala** — was devoted to the printing of popular books. Here you could get cheap editions of religious tracts and scriptures, as well as literature that was considered obscene and scandalous.

**Print and the poor people.** Very cheap small books were brought to markets in nineteenth-century Madras towns and sold at crossroads, allowing poor people travelling to markets to buy them. Public libraries were set up from the early twentieth century, expanding the access to books. These libraries were located mostly in cities and towns, and at times in prosperous villages. For rich local patrons, setting up a library was a way of acquiring prestige.

From the late nineteenth century, issues of **caste discrimination** began to be written about in many printed tracts and essays. **Jyotiba Phule**, the Maratha pioneer of 'low caste' protest movements, wrote about the injustices of the caste system in his ***Gulamgiri* (1871)**. In the twentieth century, **B.R. Ambedkar** in Maharashtra and **E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker**, better known as **Periyar**, in Madras, wrote powerfully on caste, and their writings were read by people all over India. Local protest movements and sects also created a lot of popular journals and tracts criticising ancient scriptures and envisioning a new and just future.

Workers in factories were too overworked and lacked the education to write much about their experiences. But **Kashibaba**, a Kanpur millworker, wrote and published ***Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal*** in **1938** to show the links between caste and class exploitation. The poems of another Kanpur millworker who wrote under the name of **Sudarshan Chakr** between 1935 and 1955 were brought together and published in a collection called ***Sacchi Kavitayan***. By the 1930s, Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries to educate themselves, following the example of Bombay workers.
keyTerms: Ulama — legal scholars of Islam and the sharia
Fatwa — a legal pronouncement on Islamic law
Lithography — printing from a flat stone or metal plate
Battala — area of central Calcutta famous for cheap popular books

sections.md:
Before 1798, the colonial state under the East India Company was not too concerned with censorship. Strangely, its early measures to control printed matter were directed against **Englishmen in India** who were critical of Company misrule and hated the actions of particular Company officers. The Company was worried that such criticisms might be used by its critics in England to attack its trade monopoly in India.

By the 1820s, the Calcutta Supreme Court passed certain regulations to control press freedom and the Company began encouraging publication of newspapers that would celebrate British rule. In **1835**, faced with urgent petitions by editors of English and vernacular newspapers, **Governor-General Bentinck** agreed to revise press laws. **Thomas Macaulay**, a liberal colonial official, formulated new rules that restored the earlier freedoms.

After the **revolt of 1857**, the attitude to freedom of the press changed. Enraged Englishmen demanded a clamp-down on the 'native' press. As vernacular newspapers became assertively nationalist, the colonial government began debating measures of stringent control. In **1878**, the **Vernacular Press Act** was passed, modelled on the **Irish Press Laws**. It provided the government with extensive rights to **censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press**. From now on the government kept regular track of the vernacular newspapers published in different provinces. When a report was judged as seditious, the newspaper was **warned**, and if the warning was ignored, the press was liable to be **seized and the printing machinery confiscated**.

Despite repressive measures, nationalist newspapers grew in numbers in all parts of India. They reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities. Attempts to throttle nationalist criticism provoked militant protest. This in turn led to a renewed cycle of persecution and protests. When Punjab revolutionaries were deported in **1907**, **Balgangadhar Tilak** wrote with great sympathy about them in his ***Kesari***. This led to his imprisonment in **1908**, provoking in turn widespread protests all over India.

From Gutenberg's Bible to Tilak's *Kesari*, print has been a force that frightens those in power and gives voice to those without it. That is why freedom of the press matters to every democracy, including ours.

parts.md: This story is inspired by the life of the many girls like Rashsundari Debi, but its characters are imagined. Saudamini was married at twelve into a household in East Bengal where the women rose before dawn and the kitchen fire never went out. Reading, her mother-in-law said, was for men; a girl who read would bring misfortune. Yet every morning Saudamini saw her husband's nephew chant his lessons from a little printed primer, and she began to recognise the shapes of letters the way you recognise faces in a crowd.

One day she found a single torn page of that primer near the courtyard. She hid it in the kitchen behind the spice jars. While the rice boiled she looked at it; while the fish fried she traced letters with a burnt stick on the floor and rubbed them out before anyone came. She matched sounds she had heard the boy chanting with the shapes on the page. It took her months to read a full line. When she did, she sat back on her heels, smoke in her eyes, and laughed out loud alone.

Years later, a cheap printed copy of a devotional book came into the house from a Calcutta bazaar. The men were away. Saudamini read it aloud, haltingly, to the other women in the inner courtyard. The old aunt who had once warned against reading listened with her eyes closed. When Saudamini stopped, the aunt said, 'Again, from the beginning.' Print had come to that house not as a machine but as a voice — and the voice was a woman's.

summary: The earliest print technology was woodblock hand printing in China (from AD 594), Japan and Korea; China's state printed civil service textbooks.
Japan's oldest printed book is the Diamond Sutra (AD 868); Edo's ukiyo art (Utamaro) depicted urban life.
Paper reached Europe from China in the 11th century; Marco Polo brought woodblock knowledge to Italy in 1295.
Gutenberg developed the printing press at Strasbourg in the 1430s, adapting the olive press and metal moulds; his first book was the Bible (~180 copies, 3 years).
Between 1450 and 1550 presses spread across Europe; 20 million books in the late 15th century, 200 million in the 16th.
Print created a reading public, blurring oral and reading cultures.
Luther's Ninety Five Theses (1517) spread by print and began the Reformation; the Church kept an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.
Rising literacy (60–80% in parts of Europe) led to a reading mania: chapbooks, Biliotheque Bleue, periodicals and Enlightenment writings.
Historians argue print helped create conditions for the French Revolution, though readers interpreted ideas in their own ways.
19th-century readers included children (Grimm Brothers 1812), women (Austen, Brontës, Eliot) and workers; Hoe's cylindrical press printed 8,000 sheets per hour.
Print came to India via Portuguese missionaries in Goa (mid-1500s); Hickey's Bengal Gazette began in 1780.
Print fuelled religious reform debates (Rammohun Roy's Sambad Kaumudi, Deoband fatwas, printed Ramcharitmanas 1810).
Women read and wrote more: Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban (1876), Tarabai Shinde, Pandita Ramabai.
Phule's Gulamgiri (1871), Ambedkar and Periyar wrote on caste; workers like Kashibaba wrote too.
The Vernacular Press Act (1878) allowed censorship; Tilak was imprisoned in 1908 for writing in Kesari.

rd-school-c10-social-b.p1-power-sharing.title: Power Sharing
rd-school-c10-social-b.p1-power-sharing.subtitle: Two small countries, two opposite choices — why Belgium held together and Sri Lanka slid into civil war

sections.md:
Imagine a capital city where most residents speak one language, but most people in the country speak another. Who should run the city? Who should get government jobs? Whose language goes on the signboards? Get the answer wrong and neighbours may stop trusting each other; get it badly wrong and they may take up arms.

This chapter of *Democratic Politics II* opens with exactly that dilemma, told through **two stories — Belgium and Sri Lanka**. Both are democracies. Both have communities divided by language (and, in Sri Lanka, religion). But they dealt with diversity in opposite ways, with opposite results.

From these stories we draw out the big idea of the chapter: **power sharing** — why it is good for democracy, and the different forms it takes. The plan:
1. The story of Belgium
2. The story of Sri Lanka — majoritarianism
3. Accommodation in Belgium
4. Why power sharing is desirable (prudential and moral reasons)
5. Forms of power sharing

> Keep one question in mind: *Is sharing power a weakness that slows decisions, or the very thing that keeps a country united?*

sections.h: Belgium — a small country, a complex society
sections.md:
**Belgium** is a small country in Europe, smaller in area than the state of Haryana. It borders the Netherlands, France, Germany and Luxembourg. Its population is a little over one crore (about 11 million). Its ethnic composition is very complex:

| Community | Share of country | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Dutch-speaking | about 59% | Flemish region (north) |
| French-speaking | about 40% | Wallonia (south) |
| German-speaking | about 1% | east |

In the capital, **Brussels**, the picture flips: about **80% speak French** and **20% Dutch**.

The minority French-speaking community was relatively **richer and more powerful**. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community, which got the benefit of economic development and education much later. This led to tensions between the two communities during the **1950s and 1960s**. The tension was more acute in **Brussels**, because there the Dutch-speaking people, a majority in the country, were a minority in the capital.

So Belgium had a double puzzle: the Dutch speakers could outvote the French nationally, and the French speakers dominated Brussels. Any simple 'majority wins' rule would hurt somebody.

sections.h: Sri Lanka — the path of majoritarianism
sections.md:
**Sri Lanka** is an island nation just a few kilometres off the southern coast of Tamil Nadu. It has a population of about two crore (around 20 million), roughly the same as Haryana. Like other South Asian nations it has a diverse population:

- **Sinhala speakers:** about **74%**, mostly **Buddhist**.
- **Tamil speakers:** about **18%**, divided into **Sri Lankan Tamils** (13%, natives of the country) and **Indian Tamils** (5%, whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period). Sri Lankan Tamils are concentrated in the **north and east**.
- Most Tamils are **Hindus or Muslims**; there are about **7% Christians**, who are both Tamil and Sinhala.

Sri Lanka became independent in **1948**. The leaders of the Sinhala community sought to secure dominance over government by virtue of their majority. The democratically elected government adopted a series of **majoritarian measures**:

1. In **1956**, an Act was passed to recognise **Sinhala as the only official language**, disregarding Tamil.
2. Governments followed **preferential policies** that favoured Sinhala applicants for **university positions and government jobs**.
3. A new **constitution stipulated that the state shall protect and foster Buddhism**.

### The result
All these measures, coming one after the other, gradually increased the feeling of **alienation among Sri Lankan Tamils**. They felt that none of the major political parties led by Buddhist Sinhala leaders was sensitive to their language and culture, and that the constitution and government policies denied them equal political rights, discriminated against them in jobs and other opportunities, and ignored their interests.

Relations between the communities strained over time. Sri Lankan Tamils launched parties and struggles demanding: recognition of **Tamil as an official language**, **regional autonomy**, and **equality of opportunity** in education and jobs. Their demand for more autonomy to Tamil-populated provinces was **repeatedly denied**.

By the **1980s**, several political organisations were formed demanding an **independent Tamil Eelam (state)** in the north and east. The distrust turned into widespread conflict and soon into a **civil war**. Thousands of people of both communities were killed; many families were forced to leave the country as refugees, and many more lost their livelihoods. The civil war caused a terrible setback to the social, cultural and economic life of the country. It **ended in 2009**.

**Majoritarianism** = the belief that the majority community should be able to rule a country in whichever way it wants, by disregarding the wishes and needs of the minority.

sections.md:
The Belgian leaders took a different path. They recognised the existence of regional differences and cultural diversities. Between **1970 and 1993** they **amended their constitution four times** so as to work out an arrangement that would enable everyone to live together within the same country. The Belgian model:

1. **Equal ministers at the centre:** the constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers shall be **equal** in the central government. Some special laws require the **support of a majority of members from each linguistic group**. Thus no single community can make decisions unilaterally.
2. **Powers to states:** many powers of the central government have been given to **state governments of the two regions**. State governments are **not subordinate** to the central government.
3. **Brussels:** has a **separate government** in which **both communities have equal representation**. The French-speaking people accepted equal representation in Brussels because the Dutch-speaking community had accepted equal representation in the central government.
4. **A 'community government':** a third kind of government, elected by people belonging to **one language community** — Dutch, French and German-speaking — **no matter where they live**. This government has power regarding **cultural, educational and language-related issues**.

The Belgian model is very complicated — even people living in Belgium find it hard to follow. But it has worked well. It **avoided civic strife** between the two major communities and a possible **division of the country on linguistic lines**. When many countries of Europe came together to form the **European Union**, **Brussels was chosen as its headquarters**.

### What do we learn from the two stories?
Both are democracies, but they dealt with the question of power sharing differently. In Belgium, leaders realised that unity is possible only by **respecting the feelings and interests of different communities**. Sri Lanka shows that if a majority community wants to force its dominance over others and refuses to share power, it can **undermine the unity of the country**.

sections.md:
Two different sets of reasons can be given in favour of power sharing.

### 1. Prudential reasons
Prudential means based on **careful calculation of gains and losses**.
- Power sharing is good because it helps to **reduce the possibility of conflict** between social groups.
- Since social conflict often leads to violence and **political instability**, power sharing is a good way to **ensure the stability of political order**.
- Imposing the will of the majority community over others may look like an attractive option in the short run, but in the long run it **undermines the unity** of the nation. **Tyranny of the majority** is not just oppressive for the minority; it often brings **ruin to the majority as well**.

### 2. Moral reasons
These emphasise the very act of power sharing as **valuable in itself**.
- Power sharing is the **very spirit of democracy**. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those **affected by its exercise** and who have to live with its effects.
- People have a **right to be consulted** on how they are to be governed.
- A **legitimate government** is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a **stake in the system**.

Prudential reasons stress **better outcomes**; moral reasons stress the **intrinsic worth** of sharing power.

**Exam tip:** In questions asking you to sort statements, look for words like *stability, conflict, violence, unity* (prudential) versus *spirit of democracy, right to be consulted, legitimacy* (moral).

> A boxed discussion in the textbook imagines a group of students arguing about whether sharing power is necessary only in diverse societies. Think about it: even a society with one language and religion has rich and poor, young and old, cities and villages — all of whom are affected by decisions.

check.q: 'People have a right to be consulted on how they are governed' is a:
check.why: It values power sharing for its own sake as part of democracy's spirit, not for its consequences, so it is a moral reason.

sections.md:
The old idea was that all power of a government must reside in **one person or a group of persons located at one place** — kings, or later a central authority. If power is dispersed, decisions would be hard to take and enforce. Modern democracies have **rejected** this. In a democracy people rule themselves through institutions of self-government, and political power is distributed among as many citizens as possible. Power sharing takes **four forms**:

### (a) Horizontal distribution — among organs of government
Power is shared among the **legislature, executive and judiciary**, placed at the **same level**. Each organ checks the others: ministers and government officials exercise power but are **responsible to Parliament or state assemblies**; judges are appointed by the executive but can **check the functioning of the executive or laws made by the legislature**. This is the **system of checks and balances**, which ensures no organ can exercise unlimited power.

### (b) Vertical distribution — among governments at different levels
A general government for the entire country (**Union / central / federal government**) and governments at the provincial or regional level (**state governments** in India). Such a general government with regional governments is called **federal**. In India the constitution has also created a third level, **local government** — municipalities and panchayats. Higher and lower levels of government share power.

### (c) Among different social groups
Power may be shared among **religious and linguistic groups**. The **'community government' in Belgium** is an example. In some countries there are constitutional and legal arrangements whereby socially weaker sections and women are represented in legislatures and administration — **'reserved constituencies'** in assemblies and Parliament in India. This gives space to minority communities in the government.

### (d) Among political parties, pressure groups and movements
Democracy provides citizens a choice. **Competition among parties** ensures power does not remain in one hand; in the long run power is shared among parties representing different ideologies and social groups. Sometimes power is shared directly when two or more parties form an **alliance (coalition government)**. **Interest groups** — traders, businessmen, industrialists, farmers, industrial workers — also share governmental power, by participation in governmental committees or by bringing **influence on the decision-making process**.

sections.md:
India uses every form of power sharing described above:

- **Horizontal:** Parliament makes laws, the Union Cabinet executes them, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
- **Vertical:** the Union government, 28 state governments and union territories, and lakhs of panchayats and municipal bodies (after the 1992 amendments).
- **Social groups:** reserved constituencies for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; one-third reservation for women in panchayats and municipalities.
- **Parties and pressure groups:** coalition governments have been common at the Centre since 1989; farmers' unions, trade unions and industry chambers lobby and protest.

The lesson of Belgium and Sri Lanka is not that diversity causes conflict. It is that **how a democracy handles diversity** — by sharing power or by concentrating it in the majority — decides whether diversity becomes a strength or a fault line.

> **Did you know?** Belgium once went over 500 days without a regular national government (2010–11) while parties negotiated — yet the country kept running, because so much power had been shared with regions and communities.

summary: Belgium: Dutch 59%, French 40%, German 1%; Brussels 80% French, 20% Dutch.
Tensions in the 1950s–60s arose because the richer French minority dominated and Dutch speakers were a minority in Brussels.
Sri Lanka: Sinhala 74% (mostly Buddhist), Tamils 18% (Sri Lankan 13%, Indian 5%); independent in 1948.
Majoritarian measures: 1956 Sinhala-only Act, preferential jobs/university policies, state protection of Buddhism.
Alienation led to demands for autonomy, then Tamil Eelam, then civil war that ended in 2009.
Belgium amended its constitution four times (1970–93) to accommodate communities.
Belgian model: equal ministers, special laws need each group's majority, powers to regions, equal Brussels government, community government.
Brussels became headquarters of the European Union.
Prudential reasons: power sharing reduces conflict and ensures stability.
Moral reasons: power sharing is the spirit of democracy and gives legitimacy.
Horizontal sharing among legislature, executive and judiciary — checks and balances.
Vertical sharing among union, state and local governments — federalism.
Sharing among social groups (community government, reserved constituencies) and among parties and pressure groups (coalitions, lobbying).

Examiners love precise facts. Here they are side by side.

**Belgium** (Europe; borders France, the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg). Population about 1 crore (10 million) in the NCERT account. **59%** live in the Flemish region and speak **Dutch**; **40%** live in Wallonia and speak **French**; **1%** speak **German**. In the capital **Brussels**, **80% speak French and 20% Dutch**. The French-speaking minority was richer and more powerful, which the Dutch-speaking majority resented. Between **1970 and 1993** the constitution was amended **four times**.

**Sri Lanka** (island off Tamil Nadu; independent **1948**). Population about 2 crore. **Sinhala speakers 74%**, **Tamil speakers 18%**. Tamils are of two kinds: **Sri Lankan Tamils (13%)** and **Indian Tamils (5%)**, whose forefathers came as plantation workers in the colonial period. Most Sinhalas are Buddhist; most Tamils Hindu or Muslim; about **7%** are Christian (both Tamil and Sinhala).

sections.md:
The chapter gives two sets of reasons why power sharing is good.

**Prudential reasons** (prudence = careful calculation of gains and losses): power sharing **reduces the possibility of conflict** between social groups. Social conflict often turns into violence and political instability, so sharing power is a good way to keep the political order stable. Majoritarianism looks attractive to the majority in the short run, but — as Sri Lanka shows — it undermines the unity of the nation.

**Moral reasons:** power sharing is **the very spirit of democracy**. A legitimate government is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system. People have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. So power sharing is valuable in itself, even if it did not reduce conflict.

| Prudential | Moral |
|---|---|
| Based on results/outcomes | Based on values |
| Avoids conflict and instability | Is the essence of democracy |
| Useful for the majority too, in the long run | Gives citizens their right to be consulted |

**A boxed point to remember:** an old view held that all power of a government must reside in one person or group at one place, because divided power makes decisions slow. Democracy rejects this: people are the source of all political power, and they rule themselves through institutions of self-government.

check.q: 'Power sharing reduces conflict between social groups' is a —
check.why: It is based on the careful calculation of a beneficial result — less conflict and more stability — which makes it prudential.

sections.h: Checks and balances, and the four forms with Indian examples
sections.md:
**1. Horizontal distribution** — among organs at the **same level**: legislature, executive, judiciary. Each checks the others — this is the **system of checks and balances**. In India, ministers are answerable to Parliament; judges are appointed by the executive but can check laws made by the legislature and actions of the executive.

**2. Vertical distribution** — among governments at **different levels**: Union (central) government, state governments, and local governments (panchayats and municipalities). The constitution clearly lays down powers of each level — this is **federal** division.

**3. Among social groups** — religious and linguistic groups get a share in power. Belgium's **community government** is one example; India's **reserved constituencies** for SCs and STs in legislatures are another, so that weaker sections are not left out.

**4. Among political parties, pressure groups and movements** — democracy lets parties compete, and power changes hands; sometimes it is shared directly in **coalition governments** of two or more parties. Interest groups such as traders, businessmen, industrialists, farmers and industrial workers influence decisions through participation in committees or by pressure.

**Did you know?** Because of the vertical arrangement, a citizen of Pune is governed at once by the Pune Municipal Corporation, the Government of Maharashtra and the Union Government — three levels sharing power.

check.q: Coalition governments are an example of power sharing among —
check.why: In a coalition, two or more political parties share power by forming the government together.

sections.md:
**1. What are the different forms of power sharing in modern democracies? Give an example of each.** — Horizontal (legislature, executive, judiciary in India); vertical (Union, state, local governments); among social groups (Belgium's community government, reserved seats in India); among parties and pressure groups (coalition governments, farmers' or traders' associations).

**2. State one prudential and one moral reason for power sharing with an Indian example.** — Prudential: reserved seats for SCs/STs reduce the chance of conflict by giving weaker groups a voice. Moral: the 73rd Amendment's panchayati raj gives villagers a right to be consulted on decisions about their own village.

**3. Three statements — which one reflects the true spirit of power sharing?** In NCERT's exercise, a Belgian, a Sri Lankan and an Indian student give opinions; the correct choice is the one saying power sharing **makes democracy stronger and keeps the country united** (as in Belgium), rather than one praising rule by the majority.

**4. Which of these statements about Belgium's 1993 changes is correct?** — Belgium **reduced the power of the central government and gave it to regional governments**; regional governments were given constitutional powers that were earlier with the centre.

**5. Matching forms with examples:** power shared among governments at different levels → federal government; among social groups → community government; among political parties → coalition government; among organs → separation of powers.

**6. 'Power sharing is good because it reduces conflict' vs 'it is the spirit of democracy' — which is prudential?** The first is prudential, the second moral.

**7. Why did Belgium's model work and Sri Lanka's fail?** — Belgium recognised regional and cultural diversity and gave every group a real share; Sri Lanka tried to secure dominance of one group, which bred alienation and conflict.

Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka led to distrust and a long civil war, which ended in 2009.
Belgium's model: equal ministers, powerful regional governments, a separate Brussels government and a community government.

Four forms: horizontal, vertical, among social groups, among parties/pressure groups.
Checks and balances: each organ of government keeps the others in check.

rd-school-c10-social-b.p2-federalism.subtitle: Who decides your school timings, your police, your currency and your village road? Inside India's three-tier government

sections.md:
Follow Meena, a Class 10 student in a village near Nashik, through one ordinary day. The rupee note she uses to buy a pen is issued under the authority of the **Union government**. The police constable at the bus stand works for the **Maharashtra state government**. The handpump near her house was repaired after a decision of her **gram panchayat**. Three different governments, each with its own powers, all touching one girl's day.

In the last chapter we saw that **vertical division of power** among different levels of government is one of the major forms of power sharing. This chapter studies that form, called **federalism**, in detail, in the NCERT order:
1. What is federalism? Its key features
2. What makes India a federal country?
3. How is federalism practised? (linguistic states, language policy, centre–state relations)
4. Decentralisation in India — local government

> **Did you know?** The word *federal* comes from the Latin *foedus*, meaning 'treaty' or 'covenant' — an agreement between partners.

Belgium shifted from a **unitary** to a federal form in 1993, giving powers to regional governments. Sri Lanka continues to be, for all practical purposes, a unitary system where the national government has all the powers — Tamil leaders wanted Sri Lanka to become federal.

**Federalism** is a system of government in which power is **divided between a central authority and various constituent units** of the country. Usually there are **two levels**: one for the entire country, responsible for subjects of common national interest; the other at the level of provinces or states that looks after much of the day-to-day administering of their state. Both levels **enjoy their power independent of the other**.

### Unitary vs federal
- In a **unitary system** there is either only one level of government or sub-units are **subordinate** to the central government. The central government can **pass on orders** to the provincial or local government.
- In a **federal system** the central government **cannot order the state government** to do something. State government has powers of its own for which it is not answerable to the central government. Both governments are **separately answerable to the people**.

### Key features of federalism
1. There are **two or more levels (tiers)** of government.
2. Different tiers govern the **same citizens**, but each tier has its own **jurisdiction** in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.
3. The jurisdictions of the respective levels are **specified in the constitution**, so their existence and authority are **constitutionally guaranteed**.
4. The fundamental provisions of the constitution **cannot be unilaterally changed** by one level; changes require the **consent of both levels**.
5. **Courts** have the power to interpret the constitution and the powers of different levels. The highest court acts as an **umpire** if disputes arise.
6. **Sources of revenue** for each level are clearly specified to ensure **financial autonomy**.
7. The federal system has **dual objectives**: to safeguard and promote **unity** of the country, while at the same time **accommodating regional diversity**.

The exact balance of power between the central and state governments varies from one federation to another, depending mainly on the historical context in which the federation was formed.

sections.md:
There are two kinds of routes through which federations have been formed.

### 'Coming together' federations
Independent states **come together on their own** to form a bigger unit, so that by **pooling sovereignty** and retaining identity they can increase their security. Usually the constituent states have **equal power** and are strong vis-à-vis the federal government. Examples: **USA, Switzerland, Australia**.

### 'Holding together' federations
A large country decides to **divide its power** between the constituent states and the national government. Here the **central government tends to be more powerful** vis-à-vis the states. Very often different constituent units have **unequal powers** — some units are granted special powers. Examples: **India, Spain, Belgium**.

| | Coming together | Holding together |
|---|---|---|
| How formed | independent states unite | large country divides power |
| Balance | states strong, often equal | centre stronger; units may be unequal |
| Examples | USA, Switzerland, Australia | India, Spain, Belgium |

check.q: India is an example of a:
check.why: India was a large country that chose to divide power between the Union and states, with a stronger centre — a holding-together federation.

sections.h: What makes India a federal country?
sections.md:
India emerged as an independent nation after a painful and bloody **Partition**. Soon after, several princely states became part of the country. The Constitution declared India a **Union of States**. Although it did not use the word *federation*, the Indian Union is based on the principles of federalism.

The Constitution originally provided for a **two-tier** system — the Union government (central government) and the state governments. Later, a **third tier** — **Panchayats and Municipalities** — was added.

### The three lists
The Constitution clearly provided a **threefold distribution of legislative powers**:

| List | Who makes laws | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Union List** | Union government only | defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency |
| **State List** | State governments | police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation |
| **Concurrent List** | Both Union and states | education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession |

Union List subjects are of **national importance** and need a uniform policy. State List subjects are of **state and local importance**. On Concurrent List subjects, if their laws conflict, **the law made by the Union government will prevail**.

**Residuary subjects** — those that came up after the Constitution was made and are not in any list, such as **computer software** — belong to the **Union government**.

### Not all states are equal
- Some states enjoy a **special status** (e.g. several states of the North-East have special provisions under **Article 371** for the protection of land rights, culture and preferential employment in government services). Indians who are not permanent residents cannot buy land or house in some of these areas. (Jammu and Kashmir's earlier special status under Article 370 was abolished in 2019; it was made into union territories.)
- **Union Territories** — areas too small to become independent states or which could not be merged with existing states, like **Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Delhi** — do not have the powers of a state. The central government has special powers in running them.

### Hard to change
The sharing of power between Union and states is **basic to the structure** of the Constitution. It is not easy to make changes. **Parliament cannot on its own change this arrangement.** Any change has to be passed by **both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority**, and then ratified by the legislatures of **at least half of the total states**.

### The judiciary as umpire
The judiciary plays an important role in overseeing the implementation of constitutional provisions and procedures. In case of any dispute about the division of powers, the **High Courts and the Supreme Court** make a decision. Both Union and state governments have the power to **raise resources by levying taxes**, in order to carry on the government and the responsibilities assigned to each.

sections.h: How is federalism practised? — Linguistic states
sections.md:
Constitutional provisions are necessary, but the **real success** of federalism in India can be attributed to the nature of democratic politics in the country.

### Linguistic states
The **creation of linguistic states** was the first and major test for democratic politics. Many old states vanished and many new ones were created; areas, boundaries and names changed.

In **1947**, the boundaries of several old states were changed to create new states. This was done to ensure that **people who spoke the same language lived in the same state**. Some states were created not on the basis of language but to recognise differences based on **culture, ethnicity or geography** — such as **Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand**.

When the demand for formation of states on the basis of language was raised, some national leaders **feared that it would lead to the disintegration** of the country. The central government resisted linguistic states for some time. But the experience has shown that the formation of linguistic states has actually **made the country more united**. It has also made administration easier.

(The States Reorganisation Act of **1956** was the major step in this process; Andhra State in 1953 was an early linguistic state.)

### Language policy
The second test was language policy. Our Constitution **did not give the status of national language to any one language**. **Hindi** was identified as the **official language**, but Hindi is the mother tongue of only about **40%** of Indians. Therefore there were many safeguards to protect other languages. Besides Hindi, there are **21 other languages** recognised as **Scheduled Languages** by the Constitution (22 in the Eighth Schedule in all). A candidate in an examination conducted for central government positions may opt to take the exam in any of these languages. States too have their own official languages, and much government work takes place in the official language of the concerned state.

Unlike Sri Lanka, the leaders of our country adopted a very **cautious attitude** in spreading the use of Hindi. According to the Constitution, the use of **English for official purposes was to stop in 1965**. However, many non-Hindi-speaking states demanded that English continue. In **Tamil Nadu** this movement took a violent form. The central government responded by agreeing to **continue the use of English along with Hindi** for official purposes. Promotion of Hindi continues to be the official policy, but this does not mean the central government can impose Hindi on states where people speak a different language. The **flexibility** shown by Indian political leaders helped our country avoid the kind of situation that Sri Lanka finds itself in.

sections.md:
Restructuring the Centre–State relations is one more way federalism has been strengthened in practice. How the constitutional arrangements for sharing power work depends to a large extent on **how the ruling parties and leaders follow these arrangements**.

For a long time, **the same party ruled both at the Centre and in most of the states**. This meant that the state governments did not exercise their rights as autonomous federal units. As and when the ruling party at the state level was different, the parties that ruled at the Centre tried to **undermine the power of the states**. In those days, the central government would often **misuse the Constitution to dismiss** the state governments that were controlled by rival parties. This undermined the spirit of federalism.

All this changed significantly after **1990**. This period saw the **rise of regional political parties** in many states. This was also the beginning of the era of **coalition governments** at the Centre. Since no single party got a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, the major national parties had to enter into an alliance with many parties, including several regional parties, to form a government at the Centre. This led to a new culture of **power sharing and respect for the autonomy of state governments**.

This trend was supported by a major judgement of the **Supreme Court** that made it difficult for the central government to dismiss state governments in an arbitrary manner (the S.R. Bommai case, 1994). Thus federal power sharing is more effective today than it was in the early years after the Constitution came into force.

> **Box idea from the textbook:** India has more than 1,300 mother tongues grouped under major languages (Census 2011 counted 121 languages with 10,000+ speakers). Compare this with Sri Lanka's single-language policy and see why flexibility mattered.

Federal power sharing in India needs another tier of government, below that of the state governments. This is the rationale for **decentralisation**. When power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to **local government**, it is called decentralisation.

### Why decentralise?
- There are a large number of problems and issues which are **best settled at the local level**. People have better knowledge of problems in their localities and better ideas on where to spend money and how to manage things more efficiently.
- People at the local level can **directly participate in decision making**. This helps to inculcate a habit of democratic participation. **Local government is the best way to realise one important principle of democracy, namely local self-government.**

Before 1992, local governments existed but were **directly under the control of state governments**; elections were not held regularly, and they had no powers or resources of their own.

### The 1992 Constitutional amendment
A major step towards decentralisation was taken in **1992** (73rd and 74th amendments). The Constitution was amended to make the third tier more powerful and effective:
- It is **constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections** to local government bodies.
- **Seats are reserved** in the elected bodies and the executive heads of these institutions for the **Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes**.
- **At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women.**
- An independent institution called the **State Election Commission** has been created in each state to conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
- The state governments are required to **share some powers and revenue** with local government bodies. The nature of sharing varies from state to state.

### Rural local government — Panchayati Raj
- Each village, or a group of villages in some states, has a **gram panchayat** — a council consisting of several **ward members (panch)** and a president (**sarpanch**), directly elected by all the adult population living in that ward or village. It is the decision-making body for the entire village.
- The panchayat works under the overall supervision of the **gram sabha**. All the voters in the village are its members. It has to meet at least **twice or thrice a year** to approve the annual budget of the gram panchayat and review its performance.
- A few gram panchayats are grouped together to form a **panchayat samiti** (block or mandal). Members are elected by all the panchayat members in that area.
- All the panchayat samitis or mandals in a district together constitute the **zilla (district) parishad**. Most members are elected; members of Lok Sabha and MLAs of that district and some other officials are also members. The **zilla parishad chairperson** is its political head.

### Urban local government
- **Municipalities** are set up in towns; big cities are constituted into **municipal corporations**. Both are controlled by elected bodies of people's representatives.
- The **municipal chairperson** is the political head of the municipality; in a municipal corporation the officer is called the **mayor**.

### Has it worked?
This new system of local government is the **largest experiment in democracy** conducted anywhere in the world. There are now about **36 lakh elected representatives** in the panchayats and municipalities. It has helped to deepen democracy and has increased women's representation and voice.

But difficulties remain: while elections are held regularly and enthusiastically, **gram sabhas are not held regularly**. Most state governments have **not transferred significant powers** to local governments, nor have they given **adequate resources**. We are still a long way from realising the ideal of self-government.

sections.h: Language policy: no single national language
sections.md:
Imagine a boy from Kochi and a girl from Guwahati meeting on a train. They may share no mother tongue, yet both are fully Indian. Our Constitution understood this. It did **not** give any one language the status of *the* national language.

- **Hindi** was named the *official language* of the Union, but Hindi is the mother tongue of only about 40 per cent of Indians.
- Besides Hindi, **21 other languages** are recognised as *Scheduled Languages* in the Eighth Schedule (22 in all).
- A candidate in a Central Government examination may write the paper in any of these languages.
- States have their own official languages; most state government work happens in the state's language.

The Constitution had planned that English would stop being used for official purposes in 1965. When that date came near, many non-Hindi-speaking states, especially Tamil Nadu, protested strongly. The Central Government responded by agreeing to **continue English along with Hindi** for official purposes. Promotion of Hindi remains official policy, but it cannot be *imposed* on states that speak other languages.

**Why this matters for federalism:** the flexibility shown by Indian political leaders helped the country avoid the kind of conflict seen in Sri Lanka, where one language was privileged over another. Respecting many languages made the Union stronger, not weaker.
keyTerms: Scheduled Languages — languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution
Official language — the language used for government work

sections.md:
Before 1992, local governments existed but depended on state governments, elections were irregular, and they had almost no powers or money of their own. In **1992** the Constitution was amended (the 73rd Amendment for rural areas and the 74th for urban areas) to make the **third tier** of democracy more powerful and effective.

Key provisions:
1. **Regular elections** to local bodies are now constitutionally mandatory.
2. **Reserved seats** for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes in the elected bodies and executive heads.
3. **At least one-third** of all positions are reserved for women.
4. An independent **State Election Commission** in each state conducts panchayat and municipal elections.
5. State governments must **share some powers and revenue** with local bodies; the nature of sharing varies from state to state.

Today India has one of the largest experiments in democracy anywhere: roughly 36 lakh elected representatives in panchayats and municipalities, and well over 10 lakh women among them.

check.why: The 1992 amendment reserved at least one-third of positions for women; several states have since raised it to half.

sections.h: Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies
sections.md:
**Rural local government** is called *Panchayati Raj*.

| Level | Body | Who heads it |
|---|---|---|
| Village / group of villages | Gram Panchayat | Sarpanch (president) |
| Block / mandal | Panchayat Samiti | Elected chairperson |
| District | Zilla Parishad | Chairperson |

- Each village (or group) has a **gram panchayat**: several ward members (*panch*) and a president (*sarpanch*), directly elected by all adult residents. It is the decision-making body for the village.
- The panchayat works under the overall supervision of the **gram sabha**: all voters of the village. It must meet at least twice or thrice a year to approve the annual budget and review the panchayat's work.
- A few gram panchayats form a **panchayat samiti** (block or mandal). Its members are elected by panchayat members of the area.
- All panchayat samitis of a district form the **zilla parishad**. Most of its members are elected; MPs and MLAs of the district and some district-level officers are also members.

**Urban local government:** towns have **municipalities**; big cities have **municipal corporations**. Both are controlled by elected representatives. The political head of a municipality is the *municipal chairperson*; of a corporation, the *mayor*.

sections.h: How well has local government worked?
sections.md:
Constitutional status for local government has helped **deepen democracy** and given women a real voice in politics. Women sarpanches across India have led work on drinking water, schools and roads.

But difficulties remain:
- Gram sabhas are **not held regularly** in many places.
- Most state governments have **not transferred significant powers** to local bodies.
- Local bodies often lack **adequate resources**; they depend on grants.

So we are still far from the ideal of real self-government at the grassroots. **Did you know?** Kerala's 'People's Plan' campaign in 1996 handed about a third of the state's plan funds to local bodies, an often-cited example of decentralisation done seriously.

rd-school-c10-social-b.p3-gender-religio.title: Gender, Religion and Caste
rd-school-c10-social-b.p3-gender-religio.subtitle: Three social differences, one democracy — when do they become fair demands and when do they become dangerous divisions?

sections.md:
Try this at home tonight. Make a list of every job done in your house from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. — filling water, cooking, washing utensils, dropping children to school, paying bills, sweeping, caring for an elderly grandparent. Next to each, write who did it and whether anyone was paid for it. Most families find a striking pattern.

That pattern is where this chapter begins. In the previous chapters we saw that power sharing is about accommodating differences — of region and language. Here we look at three other kinds of social differences, based on **gender, religion and caste**. In each case we ask the same questions:
- What is the nature of this division in India?
- How does it get expressed in politics?
- Do these differences lead to healthy demands — or to conflict and discrimination?

The chapter's message: social divisions are not bad in themselves. **Their political expression can be healthy** (it lets disadvantaged groups demand a fair share), **or harmful** (when one group seeks domination over others). The way democracy handles them decides the outcome.

sections.h: Gender and politics — the public/private division
sections.md:
Gender division is a form of **hierarchical social division** seen everywhere, but it is rarely recognised in the study of politics. It is often understood as natural and unchangeable. However, it is **not based on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes**.

Boys and girls are brought up to believe that the main responsibility of women is **housework and bringing up children**. This is reflected in a **sexual division of labour** in most families: women do all work inside the home such as cooking, cleaning, washing clothes, tailoring and looking after children, while men do all the work outside. It is not that men cannot do housework; they simply think it is for women. When these jobs are **paid for**, men are ready to take them up — most tailors and cooks in hotels are men.

Women do work outside the home too. In villages, women fetch water, collect fuel and work in the fields. In urban areas, poor women work as domestic helpers in middle-class homes, and middle-class women work in offices. But the majority of women's work is **not valued and does not get recognised**.

> A time-use survey idea from the textbook: on average, an Indian woman works over an hour more than an average man every day — yet much of her work is unpaid and invisible. (Exact numbers vary by survey; the pattern is consistent.)

The result of this division of labour is that although women constitute **half of humanity**, their role in public life, especially politics, is **minimal** in most societies. Earlier, only men were allowed to participate in public affairs, vote and contest for public offices.

### Feminist movements
Gradually the gender issue was raised in politics. Women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for **equal rights**: extension of **voting rights** to women, enhancing the **political and legal status** of women, improving their **educational and career opportunities**. More radical women's movements aimed at equality in **personal and family life** as well. These movements are called **feminist movements**. A **feminist** is a woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

Political expression of gender division and political mobilisation on this question helped to **improve women's role in public life**. Today women work as scientists, doctors, engineers, lawyers, managers and college teachers. In the Scandinavian countries — **Sweden, Norway and Finland** — the participation of women in public life is very high.

check.q: The sexual division of labour means:
options: Men and women share all housework equally
Housework is seen as women's work while men work outside, based on social expectations
Women are biologically unable to work outside
check.why: It is a system based on stereotypes in which women are expected to do housework and childcare while men work outside the home.

sections.h: Women in India — where the gaps are
sections.md:
In our country, women still lag much behind men despite some improvement since Independence. Ours is still a **male-dominated, patriarchal society**. *Patriarchy* literally means 'rule by father'; the concept refers to a system that values men more and gives them power over women. Women face disadvantage, discrimination and oppression in various ways:

1. **Literacy:** the literacy rate among women is only about **65%** compared with **82%** among men (Census 2011). A smaller proportion of girl students go for higher studies. When we look at school results, girls perform as well as boys and in many places better — but parents prefer to spend their resources on boys' education.
2. **Jobs:** the proportion of women among the highly paid and valued jobs is still very small. On average an Indian woman works one hour more than an average man every day, yet much of her work is not paid and therefore often not valued.
3. **Wages:** the **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** provides that equal wages should be paid to equal work. However, in almost all areas of work — sports, cinema, factories, fields — women are paid **less than men**, even when both do exactly the same work.
4. **Sex ratio:** in many parts of India parents prefer sons and find ways to have the girl child aborted (**sex-selective abortion**). This has led to a decline in the **child sex ratio** (number of girl children per thousand boys) — to **919** in 2011 — and in some states far below. Prenatal sex determination is banned by law.
5. **Safety:** there are reports of various kinds of harassment, exploitation and violence against women. Urban areas have become particularly unsafe for women. Even within the home, women face beating, harassment and other forms of domestic violence.

### Women's political representation
None of this is new, and none of it is going to change on its own. Women's organisations and activists have long held that unless women control power, their problems will not get adequate attention. One way is to have **more women as elected representatives**.

- The proportion of women in the Lok Sabha has risen slowly: it touched about **14%** of its members for the first time in **2019**; in most state assemblies it is below 5%. In this respect India is among the bottom group of nations in the world — behind several developing countries of Africa and Latin America.
- One way to solve this is to make it legally binding to have a fair proportion of women in elected bodies. This is what **Panchayati Raj** has done: **one-third of seats** in local government bodies — panchayats and municipalities — are **reserved for women**. Now there are more than **10 lakh elected women representatives** in rural and urban local bodies.
- Women's organisations long demanded similar reservation of at least one-third of seats in Lok Sabha and state assemblies. In **2023** Parliament passed the **Constitution (106th Amendment) — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**, reserving one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

Gender division is an example that some form of social division needs to be expressed in politics. It also shows that disadvantaged groups do benefit when social divisions become a political issue.

sections.md:
Religious differences are less universal than gender, but they are widespread. Many countries, including India, have followers of different religions. Unlike gender differences, religious differences are often **expressed in the field of politics**.

Some of the ways in which religion and politics relate, many of them **acceptable** in a democracy:
- **Gandhiji** used to say that religion can never be separated from politics. What he meant by religion was not any particular religion like Hinduism or Islam but the **moral values that inform all religions**. He believed politics must be guided by ethics drawn from religion.
- **Human rights groups** in our country have argued that most of the victims of communal riots are people from **religious minorities**. They demanded that the government take special steps to protect them.
- **Women's movements** have argued that **family laws** of all religions discriminate against women, and demanded that government change these laws to make them more equitable.

All these involve a relationship between religion and politics, and none of them seems very wrong. Ideas, ideals and values drawn from different religions can and perhaps should play a role in politics. People should be able to express in politics their needs, interests and demands as members of a religious community. Those in political power should be able to regulate the practice of religion so as to **prevent discrimination and oppression**. These political acts are not wrong as long as they **treat every religion equally**.

### Communalism
The problem begins when **religion is seen as the basis of the nation**. The problem becomes more acute when religion is expressed in politics in **exclusive and partisan terms**, when one religion and its followers are pitted against another. This happens when beliefs of one religion are presented as superior to those of other religions, when the demands of one religious group are formed in opposition to another, and when state power is used to establish domination of one religious group over the rest. This manner of using religion in politics is **communal politics**.

Communal politics is based on the idea that **religion is the principal basis of social community**. Followers of a particular religion must belong to one community; their fundamental interests are the same; any difference among them is irrelevant. It also follows that people of different religions cannot belong to the same social community. This belief is **fundamentally flawed**: people of one religion do not have the same interests and aspirations in every context. Everyone has several other roles, positions and identities. **There are many voices inside every community**. Communalism leads to the belief that followers of different religions cannot live as equal citizens within one nation.

### Forms communalism takes in politics
1. **Everyday beliefs** — religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities and belief in the superiority of one's religion over others. This is so common we often fail to notice it.
2. **Political dominance** — a communal mind often leads to a quest for political dominance of one's own religious community. For those in the majority, this takes the form of **majoritarian dominance**; for those in the minority, it can take the form of a desire to form a **separate political unit**.
3. **Political mobilisation on religious lines** — use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and plain fear to bring followers of one religion together in politics. In electoral politics this often involves special appeal to the interests or emotions of voters of one religion in preference to others.
4. **Communal violence, riots and massacres** — India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of Partition. The post-Independence period has also seen large-scale communal violence.

### A secular state
Communalism was and continues to be one of the major challenges to democracy in our country. The makers of our Constitution were aware of this challenge, so they chose the model of a **secular state**:
- There is **no official religion** for the Indian state. Unlike the status of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, of Islam in Pakistan, or of Christianity in England, our Constitution does not give a special status to any religion.
- The Constitution provides to all individuals and communities **freedom to profess, practise and propagate** any religion, or not to follow any.
- The Constitution **prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion**.
- At the same time, the Constitution **allows the state to intervene in the matters of religion** in order to ensure **equality within religious communities**. For example, it **bans untouchability**.

Secularism is not just an ideology of some parties or persons. It is one of the **foundations of our country**. Communalism should not be seen as a threat to some people in India; it threatens the very idea of India. That is why communalism needs to be combated — in everyday life, in religion-based mobilisation, and through informed public opinion.

sections.md:
Caste has both positive and negative aspects in politics. Let us first understand the nature of caste inequality.

Unlike gender and religion, caste division is **special to India**. All societies have some kind of social inequality and some form of division of labour. In most societies, occupations are passed on from one generation to another. **Caste system is an extreme form of this.** What makes it different from other societies is that in this system, **hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals**. Members of the same caste group were supposed to form a social community that practised the same or similar occupation, married within the caste group and did not eat with members from other caste groups.

Caste system was based on **exclusion of and discrimination against the 'outcaste' groups**. They were subjected to the inhuman practice of **untouchability**. That is why political leaders and social reformers like **Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker** advocated and worked to establish a society in which caste inequalities are absent.

Partly due to their efforts and partly due to other socio-economic changes, castes and the caste system in modern India have undergone great changes:
- With **economic development, large-scale urbanisation, growth of literacy and education, occupational mobility** and the **weakening of the position of landlords** in the villages, the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down.
- In urban areas it does not matter much who is walking along next to us on a street or eating at the next table in a restaurant.
- The Constitution of India **prohibited any caste-based discrimination** and laid the foundations of policies to reverse the injustices of the caste system.

Yet caste has not disappeared from contemporary India. Some older aspects persist: even now **most people marry within their own caste or tribe**; **untouchability has not ended completely**, despite constitutional prohibition; effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue to be felt. The caste groups that had access to education under the old system have done very well in acquiring modern education; those that did not, or were prohibited, have naturally lagged behind. That is why there is a **disproportionately large presence of 'upper caste' among the urban middle classes**. **Caste continues to be closely linked to economic status** — e.g. National Sample Survey data have repeatedly shown that the proportion of people living in poverty is much higher among Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes than among 'upper' castes.

check.q: Which reformer from Maharashtra worked against caste inequality in the 19th century?
check.why: Jotiba Phule of Maharashtra campaigned against caste discrimination and for the education of women and lower castes.

sections.h: Caste in politics and politics in caste
sections.md:
As in the case of communalism, **casteism** is rooted in the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community. Caste can take various forms in politics:

### Caste in politics
1. When parties choose candidates in elections, they keep in mind the **caste composition of the electorate** and nominate candidates from different castes so as to muster necessary support. When governments are formed, parties usually take care that representatives of different castes and tribes find a place in it.
2. Political parties and candidates **make appeals to caste sentiment** to muster support. Some parties are known to favour some castes and are seen as their representatives.
3. **Universal adult franchise** and the principle of **one-person-one-vote** compelled political leaders to gear up to the task of mobilising and securing political support. It also brought new consciousness among people of castes that were hitherto treated as inferior and low.

### But elections are not all about caste
The focus on caste in politics can sometimes give an impression that elections are all about caste and nothing else. That is far from true:
- **No parliamentary constituency in the country has a clear majority of one single caste.** So every candidate and party needs to win the confidence of more than one caste and community.
- **No party wins the votes of all the voters of a caste or community.** When people say a caste is a 'vote bank' of one party, it usually means a large proportion of the voters from that caste vote for that party.
- Many political parties may put up candidates from the same caste (if that caste is dominant). Some voters have more than one candidate from their caste, while many voters have no candidate from their caste.
- The ruling party and the sitting MP or MLA frequently **lose elections** in our country. That could not have happened if all castes and communities were frozen in their political preferences.

Voters have strong attachment to political parties which is often stronger than their attachment to caste or community. People within the same caste or community have different interests depending on their **economic condition**. Rich and poor, men and women from the same caste often vote very differently. People's assessment of the performance of the government and the popularity rating of leaders matter and are often decisive in elections.

### Politics in caste
It is not politics that gets caste-ridden; it is the **caste that gets politicised**:
1. Each caste group tries to become bigger by **incorporating neighbouring castes or sub-castes** which were earlier excluded from it.
2. Various caste groups are required to **enter into a coalition** with other castes or communities and thus enter into dialogue and negotiation.
3. New kinds of caste groups have come up in the political arena, like **'backward' and 'forward' caste groups**.

Thus caste plays different kinds of roles in politics. In some situations, expression of caste differences in politics gives many disadvantaged communities the space to **demand their share of power** — this kind of politics has helped Dalits and OBCs gain better access to decision making. Several political and non-political organisations have been demanding and agitating for an end to discrimination against particular castes, for more dignity and more access to land, resources and opportunities.

At the same time, **exclusive attention to caste can produce negative results**. Politics based on caste identity alone is not very healthy in a democracy. It can **divert attention from other pressing issues like poverty, development and corruption**. In some cases caste division leads to **tensions, conflict and even violence**.

points: Yet no constituency has one-caste majority; voters vary by class, party, performance

right.title: Politics in caste
points: Space for Dalits, OBCs to claim power — but risk of division

check.q: Which statement shows that elections are not decided by caste alone?
options: Ruling parties and sitting MPs frequently lose elections
check.why: If castes voted in fixed blocs, incumbents would rarely lose; their frequent defeat shows that performance and other issues matter.

sections.md:
| Division | Healthy expression | Harmful expression |
|---|---|---|
| Gender | demands for equal rights, reservation for women, equal pay | — (expression has mostly helped) |
| Religion | moral values in politics, protection of minorities, reform of family laws | communalism: dominance, religious mobilisation, riots |
| Caste | demands for dignity and share of power by disadvantaged castes | casteism: caste as sole identity, diversion from development, violence |

The chapter's three cases support the lesson of the whole book: social differences are a fact of every democracy. The question is not whether they will enter politics — they will — but whether democracy channels them into **fair demands** or lets them harden into **domination and conflict**. Laws matter (reservation, secular constitution, ban on untouchability), but so do everyday attitudes: the prejudice in a joke, the 'who does the dishes' question at home, the question we ask about a stranger's surname.

> **Did you know?** In 1993–94, after the 73rd Amendment, India suddenly had lakhs of women sarpanches and panch members — many of them first-time leaders — a change larger than any other democracy had attempted.

summary: Gender division is based on social expectations, not biology; it produces a sexual division of labour.
Women's work is largely unpaid and unrecognised; their role in politics was historically minimal.

India is patriarchal: female literacy ~65% vs male ~82% (2011); unequal pay despite the Equal Remuneration Act 1976; child sex ratio 919 (2011).

Religion and politics can mix acceptably when every religion is treated equally (Gandhiji's moral values, minority protection, family-law reform).
Communalism treats religion as the basis of nation and pits communities against each other.
Forms of communalism: everyday prejudice, political dominance, religious mobilisation, riots.
India is secular: no official religion, freedom of religion, no discrimination, state may intervene for equality (e.g. banning untouchability).

Urbanisation, education and the Constitution weakened caste, but endogamy, untouchability and caste-linked poverty persist.
