rd-school-c10-social-b.p4-political-part.title: Political Parties
rd-school-c10-social-b.p4-political-part.subtitle: Everyone complains about them, yet no democracy works without them — what parties do, how many we need, and how to fix them

sections.h: Imagine a country with no parties
sections.md:
Picture a Lok Sabha election where every one of the 543 constituencies has only **independent candidates**. Each promises to fix the local road. None can promise anything about national policy, because none knows who else will be elected. On results day, 543 individuals arrive in Delhi. Who becomes Prime Minister? Who decides the budget? Who is responsible if things go wrong? Nobody — and that is exactly the problem.

Political parties are the most visible institutions in a democracy. For most ordinary citizens, **democracy is equal to political parties**. Yet they are also among the **least trusted**. This chapter, the last of the 'democracy in practice' sequence, asks in NCERT order:
1. Why do we need political parties? (meaning, functions, necessity)
2. How many parties should we have? (party systems)
3. National parties and state parties in India
4. Challenges to political parties
5. How can parties be reformed?

sections.h: Meaning and functions of a political party
sections.md:
A **political party** is a **group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government**. They agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promote the **collective good**. Since there can be different views on what is good for all, parties try to persuade people why their policies are better than others. They seek to implement these policies by **winning popular support through elections**.

Parties reflect **fundamental political divisions** in a society. A party is a **part** of the society and thus involves **partisanship** — it is known by which part it stands for, which policies it supports and whose interests it upholds.

A political party has **three components**: the **leaders**, the **active members** and the **followers**.

### Functions — what do parties do?
Parties fill political offices and exercise political power by performing these functions:
1. **Contest elections.** In most democracies elections are fought mainly among the candidates put up by political parties. Parties select candidates in different ways — in the **USA** members and supporters choose candidates (primaries); in **India** **top party leaders** choose candidates.
2. **Put forward different policies and programmes**, and the voters choose from them. Each of us may have different opinions, but no government can handle such a large variety of views. Parties reduce a vast multitude of opinions into a few **basic positions**. A government is expected to base its policies on the line taken by the ruling party.
3. **Make laws for the country.** Formally, laws are debated and passed in the legislature. But since most legislators belong to a party, they go by the direction of the party leadership, irrespective of personal opinions.
4. **Form and run governments.** The big policy decisions are taken by the political executive that comes from the parties. Parties recruit leaders, train them and then make them ministers to run the government the way they want.
5. **Play the role of opposition.** Parties that lose elections voice different views and **criticise the government** for its failures or wrong policies. Opposition parties also mobilise opposition to the government.
6. **Shape public opinion.** They raise and highlight issues. Parties have lakhs of members and activists spread all over the country. Many pressure groups are extensions of parties among different sections of society. Parties sometimes launch movements for the resolution of problems faced by people.
7. **Provide access to government machinery and welfare schemes.** For an ordinary citizen it is easier to approach a local party leader than a government officer. That is why people feel close to parties even when they do not fully trust them. Parties have to be responsive to people's needs or they risk being rejected in the next election.

check.why: Unlike US primaries, Indian parties' top leadership usually decides who gets the ticket.

sections.h: Necessity — why can't we do without parties?
sections.md:
The list of functions shows why. Return to the thought experiment: if every candidate were independent, **no one would be able to make any promise to the people about any major policy change**. The government may be formed, but its **utility will remain ever uncertain**. Elected representatives will be accountable to their constituency for what they do in the locality, but **no one will be responsible for how the country is run**.

We can also test this by looking at **non-party elections to panchayats** in many states. Although parties do not contest formally, the village gets split into **factions**, each putting up a 'panel' of candidates — exactly what parties do.

That is why parties exist in almost all countries. The rise of political parties is directly linked to the **emergence of representative democracies**. As societies became large and complex, they needed some agency to **gather different views on various issues** and to present these to the government. They needed some ways to bring various representatives together so that a **responsible government** could be formed. They needed a mechanism to **support or restrain the government**, make policies, justify or oppose them. Political parties fulfil these needs.

> **Did you know?** The Election Commission of India has registered more than 2,500 political parties — but only a handful are 'recognised' national or state parties.

check.q: Why do non-party panchayat elections still produce party-like groups?
options: Villagers split into factions and put up panels of candidates
check.why: Even when parties are absent, people organise into factions to contest elections, showing that party-like organisation is necessary in a democracy.

sections.h: How many parties should we have? — Party systems
sections.md:
In a democracy any group of citizens is free to form a party. But should a country have one, two or many parties?

### One-party system
In some countries only **one party is allowed** to control and run the government. In **China**, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule. Although legally people are free to form parties, the electoral system does not permit free competition. We **cannot consider one-party systems a good option**, because this is **not a democratic option**: any democratic system must allow at least two parties to compete in elections and provide a fair chance for the competing parties to come to power.

### Two-party system
In some countries, power usually **changes between two main parties**. Several other parties may exist, contest elections and win a few seats, but only the two main parties have a serious chance of winning a majority. Examples: the **USA** (Democrats and Republicans) and the **United Kingdom** (Labour and Conservative).

### Multi-party system
When **several parties compete for power**, and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power either on their own strength or in **alliance** with others. **India** has a multi-party system.

When several parties in a multi-party system join hands for the purpose of contesting elections and winning power, it is called an **alliance or a front**. In India there were three such major alliances in the 2004 parliamentary elections — the **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)**, the **United Progressive Alliance (UPA)** and the **Left Front**. The multi-party system often appears very messy and leads to political instability. At the same time, it **allows a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation**.

### Which is best?
There is **no one ideal system** for all countries. A party system is not something any country can choose; it **evolves over a long time**, depending on the nature of society, its social and regional divisions, its history of politics and its system of elections. Each country develops a party system conditioned by its special circumstances. If India has a multi-party system, it is because the social and geographical diversity in such a large country is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties.

A textbook activity asks you to observe your own state's elections and list which parties got how many votes — try it with the latest assembly results on the ECI website.

points: Power alternates between two main parties

right.title: Multi-party system
points: Several parties can come to power, often in alliances

check.q: Why does India have a multi-party system?
options: The Constitution requires at least five parties
Its social and geographical diversity cannot be absorbed by two or three parties

sections.h: Popular participation — the box on 'parties and people'
sections.md:
The textbook includes survey evidence on how people relate to parties. In broad terms it shows that over the decades **participation in party activities has gone up in India** — the proportion of people who say they are members of a party or feel close to one has risen, and India's figures are higher than those of many older democracies such as the USA, UK, Canada and Japan. At the same time, a large share of people say they have **low trust** in parties.

So parties in India are both **criticised and needed**: people complain about them, but they also join them, attend their rallies, and approach local leaders for help. Lower-income and lower-caste groups have increasingly become active in party politics — a sign of deepening democracy.

sections.h: National and state parties in India
sections.md:
Every party in the country has to **register with the Election Commission**. The Commission treats all parties equally, but offers some special facilities to large and established parties: they are given a **unique symbol** — only official candidates of that party can use it — and they get other benefits. Parties that get this privilege are **'recognised'** by the Election Commission. That is why these parties are called **recognised political parties**.

### Criteria (as set by the Election Commission)
- **State party:** a party that secures at least **6% of the total votes** in an election to the **legislative assembly of a state** and wins at least **two seats**.
- **National party:** a party that secures at least **6% of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or assembly elections in four states** and wins at least **four seats in the Lok Sabha**. (There are alternative criteria too, such as recognition as a state party in four states.)

### National parties (as recognised by the ECI after its April 2023 review)
| Party | Founded | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)** | 1980 | revived from the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Syama Prasad Mookerjee); draws on India's ancient culture and values, Deendayal Upadhyaya's ideas of integral humanism and Antyodaya; cultural nationalism (Hindutva) important element; leader of NDA; formed governments in 1998 and since 2014 |
| **Indian National Congress (INC)** | 1885 | one of the oldest parties of the world; played a dominant role in Indian politics for several decades after Independence under Jawaharlal Nehru; centrist ideology, secularism and welfare of weaker sections; led UPA governments 2004–2014 |
| **Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP)** | 1984 | formed under the leadership of **Kanshi Ram**; seeks to represent and secure power for the **bahujan samaj** — Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities; draws inspiration from Sahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Periyar Ramaswami Naicker and Babasaheb Ambedkar; main base in Uttar Pradesh |
| **Communist Party of India (Marxist) — CPI(M)** | 1964 | believes in Marxism-Leninism; supports socialism, secularism and democracy; opposes imperialism and communalism; strong in Kerala, West Bengal (earlier) and Tripura (earlier) |
| **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)** | 2012 | emerged from an anti-corruption movement; recognised as national party in 2023; governments in Delhi and Punjab |
| **National People's Party (NPP)** | 2013 | first party from the North-East to get national status (2019); led by Conrad Sangma in Meghalaya |

(Older editions of the textbook also list CPI, NCP and the All India Trinamool Congress as national parties; they lost national status in the 2023 review but remain important state parties. Recognition can change after each election, so check the ECI website for the current list.)

### State parties
Other than these, most major parties of the country are classified as **'state parties'** — commonly called **regional parties**. Examples: Samajwadi Party, Rashtriya Janata Dal, DMK, AIADMK, Biju Janata Dal, Shiromani Akali Dal, Trinamool Congress, Telugu Desam, Shiv Sena, NCP and many more. Some of them are **all-India parties in ideology** but have succeeded only in some states.

Over the last three decades, the number and strength of these parties has expanded. This made the Parliament of India **politically more and more diverse**. **No one national party is able to secure on its own a majority** in Lok Sabha for long; as a result, national parties are compelled to form **alliances with state parties**. Since 1996 nearly every state party has got an opportunity to be a part of one or the other national-level coalition government. This has contributed to the **strengthening of federalism and democracy** in our country.

sections.md:
Popular dissatisfaction and criticism has focused on four problem areas in the working of political parties. These are not just Indian problems; parties all over the world face them.

1. **Lack of internal democracy.** All over the world there is a tendency for power to be **concentrated in one or few leaders at the top**. Parties do not keep membership registers, do not hold organisational meetings, and do not conduct internal elections regularly. Ordinary members do not get sufficient information on what happens inside the party. Those who disagree with the leadership find it difficult to continue in the party; more than loyalty to party principles, **personal loyalty to the leader** becomes important.
2. **Dynastic succession.** Since most parties do not practise open and transparent procedures, there are very few ways for an ordinary worker to rise to the top. Those who happen to be the leaders are in a position to unfairly favour people close to them, or even their **family members**. In many parties the top positions are always controlled by members of one family. This is unfair to other members and bad for democracy, since people who lack adequate experience or popular support come to occupy positions of power. This tendency is present in some measure all over the world, including in some older democracies.
3. **Growing role of money and muscle power.** Since parties are focused only on winning elections, they tend to use **shortcuts**. They nominate candidates who have or can raise lots of money. Rich people and companies who give funds to parties tend to have **influence on the policies** and decisions of the party. In some cases parties support **criminals** who can win elections. Democrats all over the world are worried about the increasing role of rich people and big companies in democratic politics.
4. **Lack of meaningful choice.** In recent years there has been a **decline in ideological differences** among parties in most parts of the world. For example, the difference between the Labour Party and the Conservative Party in Britain is very little. In our country too, the differences among major parties on economic issues have reduced. Those who want really different policies have no option. Sometimes people cannot even elect very different leaders either, because the same set of leaders keep shifting from one party to another.

check.q: When the top positions of a party are repeatedly held by members of one family, it is called:
check.why: Dynastic succession is the passing of party leadership within a family, blocking ordinary workers' rise.

sections.md:
In order to face these challenges, parties need to be reformed. Some recent efforts and suggestions in our country:

### Steps already taken
1. **Anti-defection law.** The Constitution was amended to prevent elected MLAs and MPs from **changing parties**, because many elected representatives were indulging in defection to become ministers or for cash rewards. Now the law says that if any MLA or MP changes parties, **he or she will lose the seat** in the legislature. This new law has helped bring defection down. At the same time, it has made any dissent even more difficult: MPs and MLAs have to accept whatever the party leaders decide.
2. **Affidavits.** The Supreme Court passed an order to reduce the influence of money and criminals. Now it is mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to **file an affidavit giving details of property and criminal cases** pending against them. The new system has made a lot of information available to the public. But there is no system of check on whether the information given is true. It is too early to say whether it has led to a decline in the influence of the rich and criminals.
3. **Organisational elections and income-tax returns.** The Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to **hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns**. Parties have started doing so, but sometimes only as a formality.

### Suggestions often made
- A **law to regulate the internal affairs** of parties: maintain a register of members, follow their own constitution, have an independent authority to act as a judge in party disputes, hold open elections to the highest posts.
- Make it mandatory for parties to give a **minimum number of tickets — about one-third — to women candidates**, and to have a quota for women in decision-making bodies.
- **State funding of elections**: the government should give parties money to support their election expenses, in kind (petrol, paper, telephone) or cash, on the basis of votes secured in the last election.

These have not yet been accepted. We should be careful about legal solutions: over-regulation can be counter-productive, as parties may find ways to cheat the law, and parties may not agree to laws they don't like.

### Two other ways
- **People can put pressure** on parties through petitions, publicity and agitations. Ordinary citizens, pressure groups, movements and the media can play an important role. If parties feel they will lose public support by not taking up reforms, they will become more serious.
- **Join political parties.** Parties can improve if those who want this join them. The quality of democracy depends on the degree of public participation. It is difficult to reform politics if ordinary citizens do not take part in it and simply criticise it from outside.

check.q: Under the anti-defection law, an MLA who changes party:
options: Loses the seat in the legislature
check.why: The constitutional amendment states that a legislator who defects from the party on whose ticket he or she was elected loses the seat.

summary: A political party is a group that contests elections and seeks power to implement shared policies; it has leaders, active members and followers.
Parties reflect fundamental divisions in society and involve partisanship.
Functions: contest elections, offer policies, make laws, form government, act as opposition, shape opinion, give access to welfare.
Without parties no one would be responsible for national policy; even non-party panchayat polls create factions.
One-party systems (China) are not democratic; two-party (USA, UK); multi-party (India).
Alliances or fronts form in multi-party systems: NDA, UPA, Left Front in 2004.
Party systems evolve from a country's society, history and electoral system — no single ideal.
Recognised parties get a reserved symbol; criteria are based on vote share and seats.
National parties (ECI 2023): BJP, INC, BSP, CPI(M), AAP, NPP; many strong state parties.
Coalitions with state parties since the 1990s strengthened federalism.
Challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, lack of meaningful choice.
Reforms: anti-defection law, candidate affidavits, mandatory organisational elections and tax returns.
Suggestions: regulate internal affairs, one-third tickets to women, state funding; citizens can pressure and join parties.

rd-school-c10-social-b.p5-outcomes-democ.title: Outcomes of Democracy
rd-school-c10-social-b.p5-outcomes-democ.subtitle: Democracy is slow, noisy and imperfect — so why do almost all of us still prefer it? A report card in five subjects

sections.md:
At the end of every school term you get a report card. Some subjects are excellent, some average, some need improvement — and nobody concludes that school itself should be abolished. This chapter treats **democracy** the same way.

We have studied what democracy is and how it works: power sharing, federalism, social divisions, parties. Now the final question: **what are its outcomes?** Does it deliver what it promises? The chapter grades democracy in five 'subjects':
1. Accountable, responsive and legitimate government
2. Economic growth and development
3. Reduction of inequality and poverty
4. Accommodation of social diversity
5. Dignity and freedom of the citizens

But first, a caution about how to mark the paper.

sections.h: How do we assess democracy's outcomes?

check.q: According to the chapter, democracy is best understood as:
options: A magic box that solves all problems
A form of government that creates conditions for achieving goals
A guarantee of fast economic growth
check.why: Democracy cannot achieve everything by itself; it creates conditions that citizens must use to reach their goals.

sections.md:
There are some things democracy must provide, and some it can be expected to provide.

### Accountability
Democracy ensures that people have the **right to choose their rulers** and have **control over the rulers**. Whenever possible and necessary, citizens should be able to participate in decision making that affects them all. So the most basic outcome of democracy should be that it produces a government that is **accountable to the citizens and responsive to their needs and expectations**.

### Is democracy slow?
Some people think democracy produces a less effective government. Non-democratic rulers do not have to bother about deliberation in assemblies or worry about majorities and public opinion — they can be very quick and efficient in decision making and implementation. Democracy is based on the idea of **deliberation and negotiation**. So some delay is bound to take place. But **does that make democratic government inefficient?**

Think in terms of **costs**. A non-democratic government may be very quick in taking decisions, but it may take decisions that are **not accepted by the people** and may therefore face problems. In contrast, the democratic government will take more time to follow procedures before arriving at a decision. But because it has followed procedures, its decisions may be **more acceptable to the people and more effective**. So the cost of time that democracy pays is perhaps worth it.

### Transparency
Democracy ensures that decision making will be based on **norms and procedures**. A citizen who wants to know if a decision was taken through the correct procedures can find this out — she has the **right and the means to examine the process of decision making**. This is known as **transparency**. India's **Right to Information Act (2005)** is a powerful tool of transparency. It is a factor often missing from a non-democratic government.

### Report card
- Democracies have had greater success in setting up **regular and free elections** and in setting up conditions for **open public debate** on major policies and legislation. 
- But democracies often **frustrate the needs of the people** and often ignore the demands of a majority of the population. The routine tales of **corruption** are enough to convince us that democracy is not free of this evil.
- At the same time, there is nothing to show that non-democracies are **less corrupt or more sensitive** to the people.

### Legitimacy
There is one respect in which democratic government is certainly better than its alternatives: **democratic government is a legitimate government**. It may be slow, less efficient, not always very responsive or clean, but **it is people's own government**. That is why there is an overwhelming support for the idea of democracy all over the world. The ability of democracy to generate its own support is itself an outcome that cannot be ignored.

Transparency — citizens can examine how decisions are made

check.why: Transparency means decisions follow known procedures that citizens can examine, for example through the Right to Information Act.

sections.md:
If democracies are expected to produce good governments, is it not fair to expect that they would also produce **development**? Evidence shows that in practice, many democracies did not fulfil this expectation.

If you consider all democracies and all dictatorships for the fifty years between **1950 and 2000**, **dictatorships have a slightly higher rate of economic growth** (the textbook's table compares average growth rates: roughly 4.42% for non-democracies against 3.95% for democracies, with poor democracies and poor dictatorships also compared). The inability of democracy to achieve higher economic development worries us. But this alone **cannot be reason to reject democracy**.

Economic development depends on several factors: a country's **population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, economic priorities** adopted by the country, etc. The difference in rates of economic development between less developed countries with dictatorships and democracies is **negligible**. Overall, we cannot say that democracy is a guarantee of economic development. But we can expect democracy **not to lag behind dictatorships** in this respect.

When we find such a significant difference in all cases and categories, we see that democracy is a much preferred form of government, because it has several other **positive outcomes**.

| Category (1950–2000) | Average growth (approx., as per textbook table) |
|---|---|
| All democracies | 3.95% |
| All dictatorships | 4.42% |
| Poor countries under dictatorship | 4.34% |
| Poor countries under democracy | 4.28% |

(The gap among poor countries — 4.34 vs 4.28 — is only 0.06 percentage points: negligible.)

check.q: What does the evidence on growth (1950–2000) show?
options: Dictatorships grew slightly faster overall, but among poor countries the difference is negligible
check.why: Overall dictatorships had a slightly higher growth rate, but between poor democracies and poor dictatorships the difference was tiny, so growth is no reason to reject democracy.

sections.md:
Perhaps more than development, it is reasonable to expect democracies to **reduce economic disparities**. Even when a country achieves economic growth, will wealth be distributed in such a way that all citizens of the country have a share and lead a better life?

Democracies are based on **political equality**. All individuals have equal weight in electing representatives. Parallel to the process of bringing individuals into the political arena on a free and equal basis, we find **growing economic inequalities**. A small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes. Not only that, their share in the total income of the country has been increasing. Those at the bottom of the society have very little to depend upon. Their incomes have been declining. Sometimes they find it difficult to meet their basic needs of life, such as food, clothing, house, education and health.

In actual life, democracies **do not appear to be very successful in reducing economic inequalities**. The poor constitute a large proportion of our voters and no party will like to lose their votes. Yet democratically elected governments do not appear to be as keen to address the question of poverty as you would expect them to. The situation is much worse in some other countries: in **Bangladesh**, more than half of its population lived in poverty (as per the textbook's data). People in several poor countries are now dependent on the rich countries even for food supplies.

The textbook presents data on the share of national income of the richest 20% and poorest 20% in several democracies (countries such as South Africa, Brazil, Russia, USA, UK, Denmark, Hungary). The pattern: in some democracies, like **South Africa and Brazil**, the top 20% take a very large share (over 60%) while the bottom 20% get only around 3%; in others like **Denmark and Hungary** the gap is much smaller. Democracy, by itself, does not guarantee equality — **policies** do.

**Activity type:** find out your own state's poverty data from the NITI Aayog Multidimensional Poverty Index and discuss which policies have reduced it.

check.q: Why is it puzzling that democracies have not reduced poverty more?
options: The poor are a large share of voters, yet governments are not as keen to tackle poverty as expected
Poverty does not exist in democracies
check.why: Since the poor form a large proportion of voters, one would expect parties to prioritise them, but in practice inequality has often persisted or grown.

sections.md:
Do democracies lead to peaceful and harmonious life among citizens? A democracy must fulfil one condition to be accepted: **no society can fully and permanently resolve conflicts among different groups**. But we can certainly learn to **respect these differences** and evolve mechanisms to **negotiate the differences**. Democracy is best suited to produce this outcome.

Non-democratic regimes often **turn a blind eye to or suppress internal social differences**. Ability to handle social differences, divisions and conflicts is thus a definite plus point of democratic regimes. The example of **Belgium** (Chapter 1) shows how successfully this can be done.

But this requires two conditions:
1. It is necessary to understand that **democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion**. The majority always needs to **work with the minority** so that governments function to represent the general view. Majority and minority opinions are **not permanent**.
2. It is also necessary that **rule by majority does not become rule by majority community** in terms of religion, race or linguistic group. Rule by majority means that in case of every decision or in case of every election, **different persons and groups may and can form a majority**. Democracy remains democracy only as long as **every citizen has a chance of being in majority at some point of time**. If someone is barred from being in majority on the basis of birth, then the democratic rule ceases to be accommodative for that person or group.

The example of **Sri Lanka** reminds us that a democracy must fulfil both conditions; the failure to do so can result in conflict.

check.q: Democracy remains accommodative only if:
options: The same community always forms the majority
Every citizen has a chance to be in the majority at some time
Minorities are kept out of government
check.why: Majorities must shift issue by issue; if a group is permanently barred from the majority by birth, democracy stops accommodating it.

sections.h: 5. Dignity and freedom of the citizens
sections.md:
Democracy stands much superior to any other form of government in promoting the **dignity and freedom of the individual**. Every individual wants to receive respect from fellow beings. Often conflicts arise among individuals because some feel that they are not treated with due respect. The passion for respect and freedom are the **basis of democracy**. Democracies throughout the world have recognised this, at least in principle, though to varying degrees.

### Dignity of women
Most societies across the world were historically **male-dominated**. Long struggles by women have created some sensitivity today that respect to and equal treatment of women are necessary ingredients of a democratic society. That does not mean that women are actually always treated with respect. But once the principle is recognised, it becomes easier for women to wage a struggle against what is now **unacceptable legally and morally**. In a non-democratic set-up, this unacceptability would not have legal basis because the principle of individual freedom and dignity would not have the legal and moral force there.

### Caste inequalities
The same is true of caste inequalities. Democracy in India has strengthened the claims of the **disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity**. There are instances still of caste-based inequalities and atrocities, but these **lack the moral and legal foundations**.

### Expectations rise — and that is a sign of success
Democracy is not only a set of institutions; it is a continuous process of examination. **The fact that people are complaining is itself a testimony to the success of democracy**: it shows that people have become conscious, critical and expect more. As people get some benefits of democracy, they ask for more and want to make democracy even better. A **subject** accepts what the ruler gives; a **citizen** demands. Most individuals today believe that their vote makes a difference to the way the government is run and to their own self-interest.

### The final grade
On **accountability, legitimacy, accommodation and dignity**, democracy scores clearly higher than alternatives. On **growth** it is roughly equal; on **inequality and poverty** it needs improvement. That is why the chapter concludes that democracy's outcomes, though imperfect, make it the preferred form of government — and that improving it is the citizens' task.

sections.h: Democracy vs dictatorship: the scorecard side by side
sections.md:
After looking at the five outcomes one by one, it helps to put the evidence in a single table. Remember: democracy is compared not with an imaginary perfect government, but with the **real alternatives** — dictatorships, monarchies and military rule.

The key pattern: on growth, the difference is small; on dignity, freedom, legitimacy and handling diversity, democracy wins clearly. So the case for democracy rests mostly on its **non-economic** outcomes.

head: Outcome
Democracies
Non-democracies
rows: Must answer to voters; procedures, transparency, RTI
Rulers need not answer to anyone
Faster, but often wrong and unaccepted
Guaranteed rights; struggles of women and Dalits gain legitimacy
fig.caption: Comparing outcomes; growth figures are the long-run averages reported in studies used in the textbook

check.q: On which outcome is democracy's advantage LEAST clear?
check.why: Average growth in dictatorships was slightly higher, so democracy is valued more for dignity, freedom and legitimacy than for growth.

sections.h: Expectations rise — and that is a good sign
sections.md:
A strange thing happens in democracies: the longer people live in one, the **more** they complain about it. Is that a failure?

Not really. Democracy is a continuous test. When people become *aware* of their rights, they start expecting more — clean water, fair schools, honest officials. They demand, they protest, they file RTI applications, they vote governments out. Each complaint is a **testimony to the success** of democracy: it shows people have moved from being *subjects* to being *citizens*.

A subject accepts whatever the ruler gives. A citizen believes they can influence decisions and judges those in power. In surveys across South Asia, a large majority of people say they prefer democracy and believe their vote makes a difference — even where they are unhappy with the actual performance of government.

> Dissatisfaction with *how* democracy works is not the same as rejecting democracy itself.

check.q: Why are people's complaints about democracy described as a sign of its success?
options: They prove the government is bad
They show people have become critical, aware citizens
check.why: Only citizens who know their rights and believe they can change things bother to complain and demand better.

sections.h: How to evaluate democracy: practical vs ideal
sections.md:
Two common mistakes:
1. **Expecting democracy to solve every problem** — poverty, unemployment, corruption — automatically. Democracy is only a *form of government*; it creates conditions for achieving goals. Citizens must still use those conditions.
2. **Writing democracy off** because a particular government performs badly. That judges the system by one result.

A fairer method: ask whether democracy offers **better procedures** — free and fair elections, open debate, the right to information, independent courts, a free press — and whether people can use these to correct mistakes. On these tests most democracies do better than any alternative, though they fall short of the ideal.

**Did you know?** Around the world, democracies are also more likely to transfer power peacefully, which itself prevents enormous suffering.
keyTerms: Legitimate government — one accepted as rightful by the people
Transparency — citizens can examine whether decisions followed correct procedure

sections.h: Exam corner: questions this chapter loves
sections.md:
Typical exam tasks and how to approach them:
- **'Democracies are slower in decision-making. Is this a weakness?'** Argue that the time spent on deliberation gives decisions wider acceptance and makes them more effective.
- **'Democracy has not reduced poverty. Discuss.'** Admit the evidence (the poor remain a large share of voters, yet inequality persists), then explain why democracy is still preferred.
- **Case-study passages** (a Dalit or a woman demanding rights; a minority getting a share in power) — link them to the outcome 'dignity and freedom' or 'accommodation of diversity'.
- **'Majority rule should not become rule by majority community.'** Explain that in a democracy every citizen must have a chance to be in the majority at some time; rule based on birth-based communities is not democratic.

check.q: For democracy to accommodate diversity, which condition is necessary?
options: Majority and minority opinions shift with issues
check.why: If anyone can be part of the majority on some issue, no group is permanently shut out.

summary: Democracy is judged against real alternatives, not an ideal.
Democracies are slightly behind dictatorships on average growth, but far ahead on legitimacy, dignity and freedom.
Inequality and poverty persist in many democracies — an honest weakness.
Slow decisions in democracy gain wider acceptance.
Rising expectations and complaints show people have become citizens, not subjects.
Democracy creates conditions; citizens must use them to achieve goals.
Majority rule must never mean permanent rule by one community.
Evaluate democracy by its procedures and capacity to correct itself.
practice: 'Complaints are a testimony to the success of democracy.' Explain.
Compare the economic performance of democracies and dictatorships.
Why is democracy considered a legitimate government?
How does democracy accommodate social diversity? State two conditions.
Explain the difference between a subject and a citizen.
'Democracy cannot solve every problem.' Do you agree? Give reasons.

rd-school-c10-social-c.e1-development.title: Development
rd-school-c10-social-c.e1-development.subtitle: More money, or a better life? Why different people want different things — and how we compare countries and states fairly

sections.h: What would make your life better?
sections.md:
Ask five people in your neighbourhood: *What would make your life better?*

A farmer in Vidarbha may say: more days of work, better prices for cotton, and irrigation. A girl from a rich family in Bengaluru may say: as much freedom as her brother to decide what she wants to do with her life. A daily-wage worker in Delhi may say: a regular job, a safe room, a school for his children. A family living near a planned dam may say: *don't build the dam here* — it will flood our village. A shopkeeper may say: twenty-four-hour electricity.

That is where the first chapter of *Understanding Economic Development* begins. **Development** is not one thing. The chapter, in NCERT order, asks:
1. What development promises — different people, different goals
2. Income and other goals
3. National development
4. How to compare different countries or states
5. Income and other criteria
6. Public facilities
7. Sustainability of development

The aim isn't to memorise numbers but to learn to *think* about development: what to measure, how, and what we leave out.

sections.h: What development promises — different people, different goals
sections.md:
Different persons can have **different developmental goals**, and these may be conflicting.

The textbook gives a table of categories of persons and their likely goals. In our own words:

| Category | Likely developmental goal |
|---|---|
| Landless rural labourers | more days of work and better wages; local school for children; no social discrimination; a say in village decisions |
| Prosperous farmers from Punjab | assured high family income through higher support prices for crops and hardworking, cheap labourers; settle children abroad |
| Farmers who depend only on rain | regular irrigation, fair crop prices, loans at fair interest |
| A rural woman from a land-owning family | equal treatment, freedom, safety, her own income |
| Urban unemployed youth | a job that matches education, affordable housing |
| A boy from a rich urban family | good higher education, perhaps abroad |
| A girl from a rich urban family | as much freedom as her brother; respect for her choices |
| An Adivasi from Narmada valley | secure land and forest rights; not to be displaced |

### Conflicting goals
What may be development for one may not be development for the other. It may even be **destructive** for the other. For example, industrialists may want **more dams** to get more electricity. But this may submerge the land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced — such as tribals. They might resent it and may prefer small check dams or tanks to irrigate their land.

In the same way, an extra kilometre of highway may be progress for a truck driver and a loss for the farmer whose field it cuts through.

Two things are clear: (1) different persons can have different developmental goals, and (2) what may be development for one may not be development for the other.

check.q: Why may building a big dam not be 'development' for everyone?
options: It may displace people and submerge their land and livelihoods
check.why: Industries may gain power, but families whose land is flooded lose homes and livelihoods, so the goals conflict.

sections.md:
If you look over the list of goals, you'll find one common thing: people desire **regular work, better wages, and decent prices** for their crops — **they want more income**.

But besides seeking more income, people also seek things like **equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect** of others. They resent discrimination. All these are important goals. In fact, in some cases these may be **more important** than more income or more consumption, because material goods are not all that you need to live.

Money, or material things that one can buy with it, is one factor on which our life depends. But the quality of our life also depends on **non-material things**. If it is not obvious, just think of the role of your **friends** in your life. You may desire their friendship — but you cannot buy it with money.

Similarly, there are many things that are not easily measured but mean a lot to our lives. These are often ignored. However, it would be wrong to conclude that what cannot be measured is not important.

### An example from the textbook's line of thought
If you get a job in a far-off place, before accepting it you'd consider many factors apart from income: **facilities for your family, working atmosphere, opportunity to learn**. In another case, a job may give you less pay but may offer **regular employment** that enhances your sense of security. Another job may offer high pay but no job security and also leave no time for your family. This will reduce your sense of security and freedom.

Similarly, for development, people look at a **mix of goals**. It is true that if women are engaged in paid work, their dignity in the household and society increases. However, it is also the case that if there is respect for women, there would be more sharing of housework and a greater acceptance of women working outside. A **safe and secure environment** may allow more women to take up a variety of jobs or run a business.

Hence, the developmental goals that people have are not only about better income but also about other important things in life.

check.q: Which of these is a non-material goal of development?
check.why: Freedom, respect, equal treatment and security cannot be bought with money but strongly shape the quality of life.

sections.md:
If individuals seek different goals, then their notion of **national development** is also likely to be different. If you discuss in class what India should do for development, chances are you'll hear many different ideas.

The textbook asks students to think about questions like:
- Can you think of some examples where factors other than income are important for our lives?
- What would be a fair and just path of development for all?

When we think of national development, we should keep in mind that there can be **different, even conflicting, notions** of a country's development. It is important to consider **whether there may be a better way of developing** and whether that way benefits a larger number of people. A fair and just path means:
- not ignoring the losers (displaced communities, informal workers);
- balancing income with health, education, environment and dignity;
- including future generations (sustainability — see the last section).

Democracy matters here: people's movements, debates in Parliament and courts, and public opinion shape which path the nation takes.

sections.h: How to compare different countries or states? — income
sections.md:
You might ask: if development can mean different things, how can some countries be called developed and others less developed? To compare, we pick one or more important characteristics. **Income** is considered one of the most important attributes. Countries with higher income are more developed than others with less income. This is based on the understanding that more income means more of all things human beings need. Whatever people like and will have, they'll be able to get with greater income.

### National income and average (per capita) income
The **income of the country** is the income of all the residents of the country. However, for comparison between countries, **total income is not such a useful measure**: since countries have different populations, comparing total income will not tell us what an average person is likely to earn. Hence we compare the **average income**, which is the total income of the country divided by its total population. The average income is also called **per capita income**.

**Per capita income = Total (national) income ÷ Total population**

In **World Development Reports** brought out by the **World Bank**, this criterion is used in classifying countries. Countries with high per capita income are called **rich (high-income) countries** and those with very low per capita income are **low-income countries**. India comes in the category of **lower-middle-income countries**. The rich countries, excluding countries of the Middle East and certain other small countries, are generally called **developed countries**. (The exact dollar thresholds are revised every year; check the latest World Bank classification.)

### The problem with averages
While averages are useful for comparison, they may also **hide disparities**. Consider two imaginary countries, each with five citizens:

| Citizen | Country A income (₹/month) | Country B income (₹/month) |
|---|---|---|
| I | 9,500 | 500 |
| II | 10,500 | 500 |
| III | 9,800 | 500 |
| IV | 10,000 | 500 |
| V | 10,200 | 48,000 |
| **Average** | **10,000** | **10,000** |

Both averages are ₹10,000 (A: 50,000 ÷ 5; B: 50,000 ÷ 5). Yet in Country A incomes are fairly equal, while in Country B one person is extremely rich and four are very poor. Would you rather live in A? Most people would — unless they were sure to be citizen V in B. So averages must be read together with **distribution**.

The World Bank forbids total income

sections.h: Income and other criteria — comparing states
sections.md:
When we looked at individual aspirations and goals, we found people not only think of better income but also have goals such as **security, respect for others, equal treatment, freedom** etc. Similarly, when we think about a nation or a region, we may, besides average income, think of other equally important attributes.

The textbook compares three Indian states — **Haryana, Kerala and Bihar** — on several indicators. The broad pattern (use the textbook table for exact figures):

| Indicator | Haryana | Kerala | Bihar |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per capita income | highest of the three | high (second) | lowest |
| Infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births) | moderate | **lowest** (single digits) | higher |
| Literacy rate | moderate | **highest** (about 94% in 2011) | lowest (about 62% in 2011) |
| Net attendance ratio (14–15 years) | moderate | **highest** | lowest |

Surprisingly, although **Haryana has a higher per capita income than Kerala**, Kerala is ahead in **survival of babies, literacy and school attendance**.

### Key definitions
- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):** the number of children who die before the age of **one year** as a proportion of **1,000 live children born** in that particular year.
- **Literacy Rate:** the proportion of literate population in the **7 years and above** age group.
- **Net Attendance Ratio:** the total number of children of age group **14 and 15 years attending school** as a percentage of the total number of children in the same age group.

Why is Kerala ahead? Because **money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services you may need to live well**. Income by itself is not a completely adequate indicator of material goods and services that citizens are able to use. Normally, your money cannot buy you a **pollution-free environment** or ensure that you get **unadulterated medicines**, unless you can afford to shift to a community that already has all these things. Money may also not be able to protect you from **infectious diseases**, unless the whole community takes preventive steps.

check.q: Infant mortality rate measures:
options: Deaths of children under 5 per 100 people
Children dying before age one per 1,000 live births in a year
check.why: IMR is the number of children who die before their first birthday for every 1,000 live births in that year.

sections.md:
Many of the important things that we need are **best provided collectively**. Think: will it be cheaper to have **collective security** for the whole locality or for each house to have its own security man? What if no one, other than you, in your village is interested in studying? Would you be able to study? Not unless your parents could afford to send you to some private school elsewhere. So you are actually able to study because many other children also want to study and because many people believe that the government should open schools and provide other facilities so that all children have a chance to study.

Even now, in many areas, children, particularly girls, are not able to go to secondary school because the government or society has not provided adequate facilities.

### Why Kerala does better
Kerala has a **low infant mortality rate** because it has adequate provision of **basic health and educational facilities**. Similarly, in some states, the **Public Distribution System (PDS)** functions well. Health and nutritional status of people of such states is certainly likely to be better.

### Body Mass Index (BMI) — a boxed activity
One way to find out if adults are undernourished is to calculate what nutrition scientists call **Body Mass Index (BMI)**: take the weight of the person in kg and divide it by the square of the height in metres.

**BMI = weight (kg) ÷ [height (m)]²**

If this figure is **less than 18.5** the person would be considered **undernourished**. However, if the BMI is **more than 25**, a person is **overweight**. (This criterion is for adults; children's growth needs age-specific charts. It is a rough screening tool, not a diagnosis — consult a doctor for health questions.)

Example: a person weighing 54 kg and 1.65 m tall: 1.65² = 2.7225; 54 ÷ 2.7225 ≈ 19.8 → in the normal range.

### Human Development Index (HDI)
Once it is realised that even though the level of income is important, it is an **inadequate measure** of the level of development, we begin to think of other criteria. The **Human Development Report** published by the **UNDP (United Nations Development Programme)** compares countries based on the **educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income**.

The textbook's table compares India with neighbours (Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar) on gross national income per capita (in PPP dollars), life expectancy, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling, and HDI rank. Key surprises:
- **Sri Lanka**, a much smaller country, is **far ahead of India** on HDI — well ahead in life expectancy and schooling.
- A large country like India does not have a higher rank in the world on HDI.
- India's neighbours **Nepal and Bangladesh**, with lower per capita income than India, are **not far behind India** on some indicators (like life expectancy).

Definitions:
- **Life expectancy at birth:** average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.
- **Gross Enrolment Ratio** / **mean years of schooling:** measures of schooling attained.
- **Per capita income in PPP dollars:** calculated in dollars for all countries so that it can be compared, also in such a way that every dollar would buy the same amount of goods and services in any country.

check.q: A man weighs 45 kg and is 1.60 m tall. His BMI is about:
check.why: 1.60² = 2.56 and 45 ÷ 2.56 ≈ 17.6, which is below 18.5, so he would be classed as undernourished.

sections.md:
Compared to the past, most people are much better off today. Is the present level of development **sustainable**? Increasingly, scientists warn that the present type and levels of development are not sustainable.

### Groundwater
Groundwater is an example of a **renewable resource**: it is replenished by nature, as by rain. But even renewable resources can be **overused**. For example, if we use more groundwater than what is being replenished by rain, we would be **overusing** it. The textbook cites evidence that groundwater is under serious threat of overuse in many parts of the country: about **one-third of the blocks** are overusing their groundwater reserves, and in the coming years a large share of the country's area would be taking out more than is replenished. Groundwater overuse is found particularly in the **agriculturally prosperous regions of Punjab and western Uttar Pradesh**, hard-rock plateau areas of central and south India, some coastal areas and the rapidly growing urban settlements.

### Non-renewable resources — crude oil
**Non-renewable resources** are those which will get **exhausted after years of use**. We have a fixed stock on earth which cannot be replenished. We do discover new resources that we did not know of earlier, but over time even these will get exhausted. The textbook's table on crude oil shows that at the current rate of extraction, known reserves would last only a limited number of years — and the figure is much lower for India than the world average. India therefore **imports most of its crude oil**, which makes it vulnerable to price shocks.

### Environmental degradation is not local
Consequences of environmental degradation **do not respect national or state boundaries**. This issue is no longer region- or nation-specific. Our future is linked together. **Sustainability of development** is comparatively a new area of knowledge in which scientists, economists, philosophers and other social scientists are working together.

In general, the question of development or progress is perennial. At all times, as a member of society and as individuals, we need to ask **where we want to go, what we wish to become and what our goals are**. So the debate on development continues.

> **Did you know?** Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — that is the most widely quoted definition of sustainable development, from the UN's 1987 Brundtland Report.

check.q: Groundwater is a renewable resource, yet it can be overused when:
options: It is used only for drinking
check.why: A renewable resource is sustainable only if we use it no faster than nature replenishes it.

workedExamples.q: A country has a national income of ₹1,20,000 crore and a population of 2 crore. Find its per capita income.
steps: Per capita income = national income ÷ population.

workedExamples.q: In a district, 4,800 children were born alive in a year and 48 of them died before their first birthday. Find the IMR.
steps: IMR = deaths under 1 year ÷ live births × 1,000.

summary: Different people have different and sometimes conflicting developmental goals.
What is development for one may be destructive for another (e.g. big dams and displaced people).
People seek income but also equality, freedom, security and respect; non-material goals matter.
National development involves choosing a fair and just path that benefits more people.
Income is a key comparison criterion; per capita income = total income ÷ population.
The World Bank classifies countries by per capita income; India is lower-middle income.
Averages can hide disparities; distribution matters.
Haryana has higher per capita income than Kerala, but Kerala leads on IMR, literacy and attendance.
IMR, literacy rate (7+ years) and net attendance ratio (14–15 years) measure well-being.
Many goods are best provided collectively — public health, schools, PDS.
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²; below 18.5 undernourished, above 25 overweight (adults).
UNDP's Human Development Index combines health, education and income; Sri Lanka ranks well above India.
Development must be sustainable: groundwater overuse and limited crude oil reserves are warnings.
Environmental damage crosses boundaries; the debate on development continues.

rd-school-c10-social-c.e2-sectors.subtitle: Farmer, factory worker, software engineer — how we group work, why GDP shifted to services while jobs stayed on farms, and who protects the unorganised worker

sections.h: One cup of chai, three sectors
sections.md:
Trace a cup of tea from a roadside stall in Pune. The **tea leaves** were plucked in an Assam estate. The **milk** came from a buffalo in a village outside the city. The **sugar** was made from cane in a mill in Kolhapur. The leaves were processed and packed in a factory; the sugar refined in a mill. Then **trucks** carried them, a **wholesaler** stored them, a **bank** gave the stall owner a loan, and the stall owner **served** you the chai.

That single cup involves three kinds of economic activity. This chapter, in NCERT order:
1. Sectors of economic activities — primary, secondary, tertiary
2. Comparing the three sectors — GDP and the problem of double counting
3. Historical change in sectors
4. Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors in India (rising tertiary, where are most people employed?)
5. How to create more employment
6. Division of sectors as organised and unorganised; how to protect unorganised workers
7. Sectors in terms of ownership — public and private

People are engaged in various economic activities. Some produce goods; others produce services. We classify them into groups (sectors) using some important criterion.

### Primary sector
When we produce a good by **exploiting natural resources**, it is an activity of the primary sector. Cultivation of cotton takes place within a crop season; for the growth of cotton plants we depend mainly, but not entirely, on natural factors like rainfall, sunshine and climate. The product, cotton, is a natural product. Similarly, in **dairy**, we depend on the biological process of the animals and availability of fodder. **Minerals and ores** are also natural products. Activities like **agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining** belong here. Since most of the natural products we get are from agriculture, dairy, fishing and forestry, this sector is also called **agriculture and related sector**.

### Secondary sector
Covers activities in which **natural products are changed into other forms through ways of manufacturing** that we associate with industrial activity. It is the next step after primary. The product is not produced by nature but has to be made, so some process of manufacturing is essential — in a factory, a workshop or at home. Using cotton fibre from the plant, we spin yarn and weave cloth. Using sugarcane, we make sugar or gur. We convert earth into bricks and use bricks to make houses and buildings. Since this sector gradually became associated with the different kinds of industries that came up, it is also called the **industrial sector**.

### Tertiary sector
Activities that **help in the development of the primary and secondary sectors**. These activities, by themselves, do not produce a good, but they are an **aid or a support** for the production process. Goods produced in primary or secondary sectors need to be transported by trucks or trains and sold in wholesale and retail shops. At times it may be necessary to store these in godowns. We may need to talk to others over the telephone or send letters or borrow money from banks to help production and trade. **Transport, storage, communication, banking, trade** are examples. Since these activities generate **services** rather than goods, the tertiary sector is also called the **service sector**.

The service sector also includes some essential services that may not directly help in the production of goods — **teachers, doctors, washermen, barbers, cobblers, lawyers, people doing administrative and accounting work**. In recent times, certain new services based on **information technology** such as internet cafés, ATM booths, call centres and software companies have become important.

sections.md:
The various production activities in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors result in a very large number of goods and services. Also, the three sectors have a large number of people working in them. How do we compare?

One way is to count the **value of goods and services** produced (not the number — counting 100 bags of rice and 50 cars together makes no sense). But we should **not add up the value of all goods and services**. Why? Because of **double counting**.

### The double counting problem
Suppose a farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for ₹8 per kg. The mill grinds it and sells flour to a biscuit company for ₹10 per kg. The biscuit company uses the flour and other things such as sugar and oil to make four packets of biscuits, sold in the market to consumers for ₹80 (₹20 each). Biscuits are the **final goods** — goods that reach the consumer.

Wheat and flour are **intermediate goods**: they are used up in producing the final good. The value of ₹80 for biscuits **already includes** the value of flour (₹10). Similarly, the value of all other intermediate goods is included. If we added ₹8 + ₹10 + ₹80, we would count wheat and flour twice or more.

So **only the value of final goods and services** is included. The value of final goods already includes the value of all the intermediate goods used in making them.

### GDP
The value of final goods and services produced in each sector during a particular year provides the total production of the sector for that year. The **sum of production in the three sectors** gives what is called the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** of a country. **It is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.** GDP shows how big the economy is.

In India, the task of measuring GDP is undertaken by a **central government ministry** — the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (through the National Statistical Office). This ministry, with the help of various government departments of all the Indian states and union territories, collects information relating to the total volume of goods and services and their prices and then estimates the GDP.

check.q: Why is only the value of final goods counted in GDP?
options: To avoid double counting, since final goods' value already includes intermediate goods
check.why: The price of a final good already contains the value of the inputs used, so adding inputs separately would count them twice.

sections.md:
Generally, it has been noted from the histories of many, now developed, countries that **at initial stages of development, the primary sector was the most important** sector of economic activity.

- As the methods of farming changed and the agriculture sector began to prosper, it produced **much more food** than before. Many people could now take up other activities. There were increasing numbers of craftpersons and traders. Buying and selling activities increased many times. Besides, there were also transporters, administrators, army etc. However, at this stage, most of the goods produced were natural products from the primary sector and most people were also employed in this sector.
- Over a long time (more than a hundred years), and especially because **new methods of manufacturing** were introduced, factories came up and started expanding. Those people who had earlier worked on farms now began to work in factories in large numbers. People began to use many more goods that were produced in factories at cheap rates. The **secondary sector gradually became the most important** in total production and employment. Hence, over time, a shift had taken place. This means that the importance of the sectors had changed.
- In the past 100 years, there has been a further shift from secondary to tertiary sector in developed countries. The **service sector has become the most important** in terms of total production. Most of the working people are also employed in the service sector. This is the general pattern observed in developed countries.

sections.h: Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors in India
sections.md:
The textbook shows a graph of GDP by sector for India between **1973–74 and 2013–14**. Over the forty years, while production in all three sectors has increased, it has increased the most in the **tertiary sector**. As a result, in **2013–14 the tertiary sector emerged as the largest producing sector** in India, replacing the primary sector.

### Rising importance of the tertiary sector — why?
1. **Basic services:** in any country several services such as hospitals, educational institutions, post and telegraph services, police stations, courts, village administrative offices, municipal corporations, defence, transport, banks, insurance companies etc. are required. These can be considered as basic services. In a developing country the **government** has to take responsibility for the provision of these services.
2. **Development of primary and secondary sectors** leads to the development of services such as transport, trade, storage and the like. The greater the development of the primary and secondary sectors, the more would be the demand for such services.
3. **Rising income:** as income levels rise, certain sections of people start demanding many more services like eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals, private schools, professional training etc. You can see this change quite sharply in cities.
4. **New services based on information and communication technology** have become important and essential. The production of these services has been rising rapidly.

**But** not the entire service sector is growing equally well. Service sector in India employs many different kinds of people. At one end there are a limited number of services that employ **highly skilled and educated workers**. At the other end, there are a very large number of workers engaged in services such as **small shopkeepers, repair persons, transport persons** etc. These people barely manage to earn a living, and yet they perform these services because no alternative opportunities for work are available to them. Hence, only a part of this sector is growing in importance.

### Where are most of the people employed?
The textbook compares the share of sectors in GDP and in employment (1977–78 vs 2017–18). The striking fact: although the share of the primary sector in GDP has fallen sharply (to well under a fifth), **it continues to be the largest employer** — close to half of all workers still work in agriculture and related activities. Secondary and tertiary sectors produce most of the output but employ fewer people.

Why didn't a similar shift out of the primary sector happen in employment? Because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors. Even though industrial output went up by more than eight times during the period, employment in the industry went up only around three times. The same applies to tertiary. As a result, **more than half of the workers in the country are working in the primary sector, mainly in agriculture, producing only about a quarter (now less) of the GDP**.

### Underemployment (disguised unemployment)
This means there are **more people in agriculture than is necessary**. So, even if you move a few people out, production will not be affected.

Example from the textbook: **Laxmi**, a small farmer, owns about two hectares of unirrigated land. She and her family of five work on it throughout the year. They may appear fully employed, but in fact the work they do could be done by fewer people. If two of them moved to other jobs, production on the farm would not fall, and the family's total income would rise. In this situation each person appears to be working but **no one is fully employed** — this is **underemployment** or **disguised unemployment**: the unemployment is hidden.

Underemployment can also happen in other sectors. In cities there are thousands of casual workers in the service sector who search for daily employment — painters, plumbers, repair persons. Many of them don't find work every day. Others, like street vendors pushing carts or selling things, may spend the whole day but earn very little.

sections.md:
From the above discussion, there is underemployment in agriculture and there are also people who are not employed at all. How can we increase employment for people? Some of the ways the textbook discusses:

1. **Irrigation and small works:** take Laxmi's case. If a **well** is dug or a **check dam** built, she could grow a second crop. More people would be employed in her own farm. A study cited points to the potential of tens of lakhs of jobs if water resources are developed, and canals etc. built by government.
2. **Rural roads and storage:** if a farmer in a remote village got a loan from a bank and had a road and transport, he could sell produce in a bigger town at a better price. Investment in **transportation and storage** (e.g. a **cold storage**) creates jobs not only for farmers but also for others in services like transport or trade.
3. **Cheap credit:** with a bank loan at a reasonable interest rate, Laxmi could buy seeds, fertilisers and pumps, increasing productivity.
4. **Agro-processing and small industries** in semi-rural areas: e.g. setting up a **dal mill**, a cold storage, honey collection, vegetable and fruit processing in the area where crops are grown. Such industries can employ many people.
5. **Tourism, regional craft industry, IT** — the textbook notes that every state has potential to increase income and employment through tourism; a study suggests a large number of jobs could be created in **education and health** too (more teachers, doctors, nurses, health workers in rural areas).

### MGNREGA 2005
The central government in India made a law implementing the **Right to Work** in about 625 districts. It is called the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA 2005)**:
- All those who are able to, and are in need of, work in rural areas are **guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year** by the government.
- If the government fails in its duty to provide employment, it will give **unemployment allowances** to the people.
- The types of work that would in future help to increase production from land will be given preference.
- **One-third** of the proposed jobs are reserved for **women**.

check.q: Under MGNREGA, how many days of work are guaranteed per rural household per year?
check.why: The Act guarantees 100 days of wage employment a year to rural households that need work, with an allowance if work is not provided.

sections.h: Division of sectors as organised and unorganised
sections.md:
Another way of classifying economic activities is by looking at the way people are employed — their working conditions.

### Organised sector
Covers those enterprises or places of work where the **terms of employment are regular** and therefore people have **assured work**. They are **registered by the government** and have to follow its rules and regulations, which are given in various laws such as the **Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act, Shops and Establishments Act** etc. It is called organised because it has some **formal processes and procedures**.

Workers in the organised sector enjoy **security of employment**. They are expected to work only a **fixed number of hours**; if they work more, they get **overtime**. They also get **paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity** etc. They are supposed to get **medical benefits** and, under the laws, the factory manager has to ensure facilities like drinking water and a safe working environment. When they retire, many get **pensions**.

**Example (textbook):** Kanta works in an office and goes at 9.30 a.m. and returns at 5.30 p.m. She gets her salary regularly at the end of every month. In addition she gets provident fund as per the government's rules, medical and other allowances, leave on Sundays, paid holidays, and her appointment letter states all terms of employment.

### Unorganised sector
Characterised by **small and scattered units** which are **largely outside the control of the government**. There are rules and regulations but these are **not followed**. Jobs here are **low-paid and often not regular**. There is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays, leave due to sickness etc. **Employment is not secure**. People can be asked to leave without any reason. When there is less work, such as during some seasons, some people may be asked to leave. A lot also depends on the whims of the employer. This sector includes a large number of people who are employed on their own, doing small jobs such as selling on the street or doing repair work. Similarly, farmers work on their own and hire labourers as and when they require.

**Example:** Kamal works as a daily wage labourer in a nearby grocery shop. He goes at 7.30 a.m. and works till 8.00 p.m. He gets no other allowance apart from his wages. He is not given paid leave or holidays. He has no letter of appointment.

### How to protect workers in the unorganised sector?
The organised sector offers jobs that are the most sought after. But the employment opportunities in the organised sector have been expanding very slowly. Many organised-sector units now also hire workers on contract, without the protections. Meanwhile, a large number of workers are forced to enter the unorganised sector, where jobs are very low-paying.

Who needs protection?
- **Rural areas:** landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans (weavers, blacksmiths, carpenters, goldsmiths). Nearly **80% of rural households** in India are in the small and marginal farmer category. These farmers need to be supported through adequate facilities for **timely delivery of seeds, agricultural inputs, credit, storage facilities and marketing outlets**.
- **Urban areas:** workers in **small-scale industry**, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, and those who work as street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers, rag pickers etc. Small-scale industry needs the government's support for procuring raw material and marketing of output. Casual workers need protection in terms of wages and job security.
- A majority of workers from **scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities** find themselves in the unorganised sector; besides getting irregular and low-paid work, they also face **social discrimination**. Protection and support therefore require economic and social development.
